status: Partial. Assembled from the research run's own output files after the final merge step stalled. Every rule below was written and adversarially fact checked; the merge was only ever going to reorder them.
disclaimer: Deterministic rules for an AWS advisory engine. Certainty levels are honest: HARD_LIMIT means a documented AWS quota or a physical fact, STRONG means near universal practice, CONTEXTUAL means it depends and the conditions are stated. Not affiliated with AWS. Verify against the linked source before acting.

rules.rule: IF environment=production AND the compute tier (EC2 fleet, ASG, ECS service, EKS node group) is confined to one Availability Zone THEN FAIL: spread it across >=2 AZs AND verify that its state is not AZ-bound.
rules.plain: Production servers must run in at least two data-centre zones. Check the data too: a disk that lives in one zone pins you there even if the servers are spread.
rules.why: A single-AZ compute tier is an unmitigated single point of failure. The AWS Compute SLA commits 99.99% at the Region level and only 99.5% for a single EC2 instance under the Instance-Level SLA, and the credit never covers lost revenue. The SLA tier you fall under is a property of the architecture, not of AZ count alone.
rules.trigger: environment=production AND distinct_az_count(compute_tier)<2
rules.exception: Stateless batch that can be re-run, and workloads pinned by a hardware dependency (single-AZ FSx for Lustre scratch, per-socket licensing, sub-millisecond placement groups). Spreading compute without addressing data placement is a false pass: EBS volumes and instance-store state are AZ-bound.

rules.rule: IF environment=production AND resource IN (RDS, Aurora, ElastiCache, OpenSearch, MSK) AND (multi_az=false OR subnet_group_az_count<2 OR (engine=ElastiCache AND automatic_failover=false)) THEN FAIL.
rules.plain: Production databases and caches must span two zones, the subnet group must actually contain two zones, and ElastiCache needs automatic failover switched on as a separate setting.
rules.why: The trap is a resource that looks Multi-AZ-capable while its subnet group holds one AZ, so there is no failover target. Single-AZ RDS recovery means restore-from-snapshot, typically tens of minutes to hours, against roughly 60 seconds for a Multi-AZ failover. For ElastiCache, subnets in two AZs without automatic failover is still a manual recovery.
rules.trigger: environment=production AND resource_type IN (rds,aurora,elasticache,opensearch,msk) AND (multi_az=false OR subnet_group.az_count<2 OR (elasticache AND auto_failover_enabled=false))
rules.exception: A cache or search index that is a pure derived copy rebuildable from source inside the stated RTO. Note an ALB cannot be created with fewer than two subnets in two AZs, so it is not part of this check; for load balancers the real questions are cross-zone settings and unhealthy-AZ behaviour.

rules.rule: IF the requirement is availability THEN use Multi-AZ (synchronous standby, automatic failover, standby not readable on the single-standby deployment). IF the requirement is read scaling THEN use read replicas. Never substitute one for the other; a design needing both needs both.
rules.plain: Multi-AZ protects you from a dead zone. Read replicas take load off the primary. They are different products and a read replica will not automatically save you in an outage.
rules.why: A read replica is asynchronous: promoting it after a primary failure can lose committed transactions and requires an operator. Teams pay for one and assume they got both. Read replicas also do nothing for write throughput, storage IOPS or lock contention, and on RDS each replica replays the full write stream.
rules.trigger: (availability_requirement=true AND multi_az=false AND read_replica_count>0) OR (bottleneck IN (writes,iops,lock_contention) AND proposed_fix=read_replica)
rules.exception: RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster deployments give two readable standbys and serve both purposes. Aurora Replicas read the same 6-copy/3-AZ cluster volume, so they add read capacity without adding write amplification and are also failover targets. RDS for MySQL, MariaDB and PostgreSQL now support up to 15 read replicas (5 remains the figure for Oracle and SQL Server); Aurora supports 15. Read-after-write traffic must still go to the writer.

rules.rule: Select the DR strategy from measured RTO/RPO against the AWS bands: Backup and Restore (RPO hours, RTO 24h or less); Pilot Light (RPO minutes, RTO tens of minutes); Warm Standby (RPO seconds, RTO minutes); Multi-Site active/active (RPO near zero, RTO near real time). Multi-AZ alone NEVER satisfies a regional-failure RTO.
rules.plain: Pick your disaster-recovery shape from how fast you must be back and how much data you can lose. Zone redundancy does not survive a region failure; only a second region does, and it roughly doubles the bill.
rules.why: Each step up multiplies steady-state spend, and the dominant new line items in active/active are inter-Region data transfer and global-database replication, not compute. Teams routinely pay active/active prices for a warm-standby requirement, or claim region resilience while running Multi-AZ only.
rules.trigger: dr_strategy NOT IN band(rto_target,rpo_target) OR (regional_failure_in_threat_model=true AND region_count=1)
rules.exception: Regulatory mandates can force multi-Region regardless of the RTO maths. Conversely a workload whose data is fully reconstructable upstream tolerates a far worse RPO than its owner first claims. The numeric cut-offs between bands are not published by AWS; do not quote invented hour thresholds as AWS guidance.

rules.rule: IF surviving capacity after an AZ or Region loss would have to scale out, launch, or mutate configuration before it can serve full load THEN the design is not statically stable. Pre-provision so survivors carry 100% of peak with zero mutating actions: across N AZs, size each at 1/(N-1) of total (3 AZs => ~50% each, ~150% total).
rules.plain: Do not plan to buy more servers during the outage. Have the spare capacity already running so losing a zone changes nothing you have to do.
rules.why: Control planes are the most complex and least available part of any system and are under maximum stress precisely when everyone fails over at once. On 20 Oct 2025 new EC2 launches stayed broken for hours after the root cause was fixed; fleets already running rode it out, fleets that needed to grow did not. This is the single most important resilience property AWS publishes.
rules.trigger: az_count>=2 AND per_az_provisioned_capacity_pct < 100/(az_count-1)
rules.exception: Batch and async workloads that can accept a backlog and drain later. The cost is explicit: three-AZ static stability is roughly 50% over-provisioning, and it applies to pre-created targets, pre-warmed connections and pre-allocated IPs as well as to instances.

rules.rule: IF any step on the critical path of a failover MUTATES state through a control-plane API (RunInstances, CreateStack, UpdateService, RegisterTargets, ChangeResourceRecordSets, Global Accelerator traffic dial, quota increase) THEN rework it: the step must be pre-executed or replaced by a data-plane action on pre-provisioned capacity.
rules.plain: During a big outage the part of AWS that creates and changes things is the part most likely to be broken. Failover must only use things that already exist.
rules.why: AWS designs data planes to a higher availability goal than control planes and states this explicitly. On 7 Dec 2021 the EC2, ELB, Route 53, STS and Console control planes were impaired in us-east-1 while running instances and existing data planes kept serving. A plan whose first step is launch the standby fails exactly when it is needed.
rules.trigger: failover_runbook.steps ANY (step.api_class=control_plane AND step.mutates=true AND step.on_critical_path=true)
rules.exception: Explicitly data-plane and therefore permitted: Route 53 Application Recovery Controller routing-control state changes, Route 53 health-check-driven failover on pre-created records, Global Accelerator endpoint health-based failover on pre-provisioned endpoint groups, ARC zonal shift, and DynamoDB global-table or Aurora Global Database writes. Warm standby deliberately trades some of this away by relying on Auto Scaling; that is acceptable only if pre-provisioned capacity alone meets the RTO. ARC clusters are a paid, multi-Region construct and must be created in advance.

rules.rule: Changes to IAM, Organizations, CloudFront, Route 53 public hosted zones and ACM certificates for CloudFront are made only through the us-east-1 endpoint. IF a failover plan must CHANGE any of those at failover time THEN pre-create and pre-stage the resource instead.
rules.plain: IAM, CloudFront and Route 53 records are only steerable from Northern Virginia. Do not plan to change them during an outage.
rules.why: Teams outside us-east-1 who believed they were unaffected discovered their failover required an IAM role change or a DNS record change they could not make. Be precise about what this does and does not mean: IAM writes are us-east-1 backed while IAM authorization is regional and kept serving in both the Dec 2021 and Oct 2025 events, and Route 53 authoritative resolution is a globally distributed data plane; only zone CHANGES are us-east-1.
rules.trigger: failover_plan.calls ANY api IN (iam:Create*,iam:Put*,iam:Update*,organizations:*,cloudfront:Update*,route53:ChangeResourceRecordSets,acm:RequestCertificate) AND resource_precreated=false
rules.exception: Use regional STS endpoints rather than the legacy global endpoint, and pre-create ARC routing controls and health-check-based Route 53 failover records, which are data-plane and usable during a us-east-1 control-plane event.

rules.rule: IF region_count>1 AND any component on the critical path exists in one Region only (identity/SSO tenant, CI/CD pipeline, Terraform state bucket, single-Region KMS key, secrets store, observability stack, container registry, the Route 53 zone you must change) THEN effective availability is that of the shared component, not of the Regions.
rules.plain: Two regions do not help if both depend on the same one thing in the middle. Write the list of shared components down; do not assert independence.
rules.why: The Dec 2021 and Oct 2025 events hit companies who believed they were multi-Region: their deploy pipeline, secrets or identity provider lived in us-east-1, so they could not deploy, authenticate or steer traffic even though the other Region was healthy.
rules.trigger: region_count>1 AND EXISTS component WHERE component.region_count=1 AND component.on_critical_path=true
rules.exception: A shared component genuinely off the failover path (a monthly billing job) may remain single-Region if that is documented and the dependency direction is proven.

rules.rule: For every quota on the failover path assert quota(dr_region) >= projected_failover_peak (NOT current usage, which in an idle standby is near zero), and separately assert that capacity will exist: hold On-Demand Capacity Reservations or a capacity-aware instance-type mix. Quotas are per account AND per Region and are not replicated.
rules.plain: Raise your limits in the standby region before the emergency, because you may not be able to raise them during it. And a limit is not capacity: the instance type may simply be unavailable on the day.
rules.why: AWS states plainly that you must ensure DR-Region quotas are high enough not to limit scaling to production capacity. This is the most common way a rehearsed failover stalls part way. Quota increases are themselves a control-plane request; many are now automatic within minutes but not all, and no quota check ever detects an InsufficientInstanceCapacity error.
rules.trigger: dr_region_exists=true AND EXISTS quota ON failover_path WHERE applied_quota < projected_failover_peak_usage, OR capacity_reservation_absent AND instance_type_diversity<2
rules.exception: A backup-only Region storing snapshots with an RTO measured in days may raise compute quotas at failover time if the runbook says so explicitly and the lead time is inside the RTO. Alarm on Service Quotas CloudWatch usage metrics at a chosen share of applied quota (70-80% is our convention, not AWS guidance).

rules.rule: IF a multi-region failover has never been executed end to end against production traffic within the stated exercise interval THEN treat the second Region as unproven capacity, not as DR. The plan's status is the date of its last full test, not of its last document review.
rules.plain: If you have never actually failed over for real, you do not have a DR plan, you have a document.
rules.why: Untested evacuations fail on the boring parts: standby quotas sized for idle, an AMI or container image never copied, a single-Region KMS key, a secret that exists only in the primary, replication lag nobody measured, and a runbook step that needs a control-plane API which is down. Each is only discoverable by doing it.
rules.trigger: multi_region_claimed=true AND days_since_full_failover_exercise>exercise_interval_days
rules.exception: Workloads with a stated RTO in days may substitute a documented restore-plus-smoke-test. The 180-day interval commonly used is a convention, not an AWS number; pick it from your change rate. Failback is the harder half and must be exercised too.

rules.rule: IF the design claims tolerance of AZ loss, instance loss, dependency timeout, dependency grey failure, credential or certificate expiry, or a scale-out event THEN each claim MUST be validated by an AWS Fault Injection Service experiment with a stated steady-state hypothesis and an automatic stop condition bound to a CloudWatch alarm. Separately, IF the system has never been fully cold-restarted THEN its recovery-time estimate is unverified.
rules.plain: Break it on purpose in a test environment before reality does it for you, with an automatic abort. And if you have never restarted the whole thing from cold, you do not know how long recovery takes.
rules.why: Untested runbooks fail on stale IPs, revoked access, missing on-call permissions and steps that assume a console which is down. In the 28 Feb 2017 S3 event the index subsystem had not been fully restarted in years and the safety checks took far longer than anyone expected, which is what turned minutes into hours. An experiment you cannot halt is an outage you scheduled.
rules.trigger: resilience_claim_exists AND (fis_experiment_template_count=0 OR fis_experiment.stop_condition IS NULL) OR days_since_full_cold_restart>365
rules.exception: Start in pre-production; production injection needs mature observability and rollback first. Some failure modes (full Region loss, control-plane failure) cannot be faithfully injected and must be reasoned about plus exercised as a real evacuation drill. Immutable fleets restarted by every deploy already measure cold-start time continuously.

rules.rule: IF one shared stack serves all customers AND a poison input or hot tenant can affect all of them THEN split into cells: independent full stacks each serving a bounded subset, with a routing layer far simpler than the cells and no shared data plane, deployed cell by cell. Where customers must share a worker pool, assign each a RANDOM COMBINATION of workers (shuffle sharding) rather than a contiguous block.
rules.plain: Run several complete smaller copies instead of one big system, and give each customer a random set of workers. Then a bad release or a bad customer only breaks a slice.
rules.why: Cells convert a 100%-impact event into a 1/N-impact event and give a safe deployment unit and a bounded restart time, which is what AWS itself adopted after the 2017 and 2020 events. Shuffle sharding gets the isolation for free from combinatorics: with 8 workers and 2 per customer there are 28 combinations, so one abusive customer fully overlaps only about 1/28 of the others.
rules.trigger: (cell_count=1 AND (tenant_count>1000 OR availability_target>=99.95)) OR (multi_tenant=true AND shard_assignment=contiguous)
rules.exception: Cells multiply fixed costs (a database, load balancer and monitoring stack each) and make cross-tenant features hard; below a few hundred tenants or a 99.9% target the overhead usually is not justified. Shuffle sharding needs a stateless pool and a client that retries across its assigned workers; it does not apply to data sharding where each shard owns distinct data.

rules.rule: IF any mechanism can mutate production capacity or shared control state - an operator runbook command, a self-healing job, an auto-remediation, a DNS or routing planner - THEN it MUST have all of: a cap on the fraction of a fleet it can touch per invocation AND an absolute minimum-remaining floor; a minimum-capacity guard; a stale-write or generation check; a change rate limit; a staged rollout across cells; and a kill switch that works WITHOUT the system being stopped.
rules.plain: Any tool or robot that can take capacity away or change shared settings needs a speed limit, a floor it cannot go below, a lock against stale writes, and an off switch that works when it is misbehaving.
rules.why: On 28 Feb 2017 an authorized operator running an established playbook mistyped a parameter and removed far more S3 servers than intended, including the index and placement subsystems; AWS's remediation was to make the tool remove capacity more slowly and refuse to go below minimum capacity. On 20 Oct 2025 a DynamoDB DNS Planner and Enactor raced, a delayed Enactor applied a stale plan while cleanup deleted it, the regional endpoint was left with no DNS records, and AWS disabled the automation worldwide.
rules.trigger: mutator.mutates_production_or_shared_state=true AND (max_fraction_per_invocation IS NULL OR min_remaining_floor IS NULL OR stale_write_check=false OR change_rate_limit IS NULL OR kill_switch_independent=false)
rules.exception: A declared, announced fleet-wide drain (Region decommission, game day) under two-person approval may exceed the cap. Idempotent additive automations (tagging, log shipping) may skip the approval gate but still need the rate limit. The kill switch is never exempt, and must itself be exercised on a schedule. A percentage cap alone is wrong on small fleets - 10% of 2 hosts is still half of them.

rules.rule: IF a component builds an in-memory routing, config or shard map from a remote source THEN an empty or partial result MUST be rejected and the previous good map retained (fail static), with a minimum-entry validation. IF a security or compliance scan returns zero findings or zero resources THEN it MUST be validated before it is reported as clean.
rules.plain: If the config you fetch comes back empty, keep the old one. Empty is a bug, not an answer. The same goes for a scan that finds nothing.
rules.why: Kinesis front-ends in Nov 2020 ended up with useless shard-maps from failed cache construction and could not route; on 20 Oct 2025 DynamoDB DNS automation left an empty record for the regional endpoint and everything downstream believed the emptiness. On the verification side, a missing IAM permission, a disabled Config recorder, an unenumerated Region or a paginator that stopped at page one all present identically to clean.
rules.trigger: config_load.on_empty_result != retain_previous OR config_load.min_entries IS NULL OR (scan.findings_count=0 AND scan.resources_enumerated_count IS NULL)
rules.exception: A genuine scale-to-zero system where zero entries is legitimate must signal that explicitly rather than let it be inferred from an empty payload. For scans, the cheap and always-available control is to assert a non-zero enumerated resource count plus pagination-complete plus recorder-status before reporting; a deliberately non-compliant canary resource is better but may be blocked by the very SCPs this base mandates.

rules.rule: IF per-host resource cost grows with fleet size (threads or sockets per peer, O(n^2) gossip, full-mesh caches, connection fan-out) THEN emit a metric of that resource against its OS or configuration ceiling and alarm well below it; do not assume adding capacity is safe.
rules.plain: Some systems get less stable as you add servers. Measure the hidden ceiling instead of just adding machines.
rules.why: On 25 Nov 2020 each Kinesis front-end created OS threads for every other front-end, so adding capacity pushed the whole fleet past the operating-system thread limit, shard-map construction failed and the fleet could not route. AWS's fix was fewer, larger servers plus alarming on thread consumption. Adding capacity caused the outage.
rules.trigger: (architecture=full_mesh OR per_peer_resource_allocation=true) AND ceiling_metric_alarm=false
rules.exception: Shared-nothing fleets with no peer-to-peer state, where per-host cost is independent of fleet size. Note this is an OS or configuration ceiling, not an AWS service quota, and is therefore invisible to Service Quotas tooling.

rules.rule: IF two nodes can both believe they are the writer THEN leader election MUST use a quorum store of >=3 members PLUS a monotonically increasing fencing token that the STORAGE layer checks and rejects. A lease or heartbeat alone does not prevent split brain.
rules.plain: A leader can freeze, lose its turn, wake up and keep writing. The storage must refuse the stale leader by number.
rules.why: Timeouts cannot distinguish a dead node from a slow one, and GC pauses, VM freezes and network partitions all produce the slow-node-that-returns case. Without a token rejected at the resource, both leaders write and the corruption is silent until a reconciliation finds it. Two-node clusters can never reach quorum and are the classic split-brain shape.
rules.trigger: leader_election=true AND (quorum_size<3 OR fencing_token_enforced_at_storage=false)
rules.exception: Designs where the storage itself enforces exclusivity - DynamoDB conditional writes on a version attribute, S3 conditional writes with If-Match/If-None-Match, a single RDS primary - because there the database IS the fencing mechanism.

rules.rule: IF the status page, health dashboard, alerting path or incident comms channel has a runtime dependency on the system it reports on THEN it is a circular dependency. The external comms path MUST live in a different failure domain - preferably a different provider, with different DNS and registrar - and MUST be servable statically with no dynamic backend.
rules.plain: Your outage page must not be hosted on the thing that goes down, and it must not need a working backend to render.
rules.why: In Feb 2017 the AWS Service Health Dashboard could not be updated because its admin console depended on the S3 that was down. In Dec 2021 impaired internal monitoring and a Console dependency delayed both diagnosis and customer notification. Moving to another Region of the same provider is not enough: identity, DNS and global control planes are still shared.
rules.trigger: status_page.failure_domain == monitored_service.failure_domain OR alerting_pipeline.depends_on(monitored_service)=true OR status_page.requires_dynamic_backend=true
rules.exception: A mandated in-product or regulated notification channel that must live in-estate needs a pre-staged out-of-band fallback (static host plus SMS or phone tree) as the compensating control. Internal dashboards may share the domain if a degraded-mode fallback exists elsewhere.

rules.rule: IF cross-region or cross-account replication is enabled THEN it does NOT satisfy the backup requirement: assert a per-datastore point-in-time control - RDS/Aurora PITR, DynamoDB PITR, AWS Backup continuous backup, S3 Object Lock or a logically air-gapped vault. Test the S3 flag against S3 datastores and the PITR flag against databases, never both against everything.
rules.plain: Copying data to another region does not protect you from someone deleting or corrupting it - the damage copies too. You still need point-in-time recovery and an immutable copy.
rules.why: AWS states continuous replication may not protect against data corruption or malicious deletion as well as point-in-time backups do. Replication faithfully propagates a DROP TABLE or a ransomware encryption pass. The recovery point for a data disaster is always some time before discovery, never zero. S3 versioning is NOT point-in-time recovery: it protects against overwrite and delete but gives no consistent cross-object restore point and no defence against a lifecycle expiry or a permanent delete by a credential holder.
rules.trigger: replication_enabled=true AND ((datastore=s3 AND object_lock_or_airgapped_vault=false) OR (datastore IN (rds,aurora,dynamodb) AND pitr_enabled=false))
rules.exception: S3 replication is partly self-protecting: by default a delete in the source adds a delete marker in the source only and delete-marker replication is off, so the replica keeps the object. That mitigates deletes, not overwrites or corruption.

rules.rule: IF a backup has never been restored to a throwaway target and byte- or row-compared, OR the restore test is older than the chosen interval, THEN it is not a backup and its RTO is unproven. Require an AWS Backup restore testing plan, a copy in a SEPARATE ACCOUNT with its own credentials, an immutable copy (Backup Vault Lock or S3 Object Lock in compliance mode), and a key owned by the backup account. Measure restore DURATION against RTO, not just success.
rules.plain: A backup you have never restored is not a backup. Keep a copy in another account, make it impossible to delete, and time the restore.
rules.why: The failure is never the snapshot job; it is that the snapshot excluded a volume, the KMS key lives in the account that was deleted, cross-account grants were missing, or nobody knows the procedure. AWS Backup has had scheduled, automated restore testing with optional Lambda validation and automatic cleanup since Nov 2023 across EBS, EC2, RDS, Aurora, EFS, S3, DynamoDB, FSx, DocumentDB and Neptune, so there is no longer an argument that restore cannot be automated. Restore is itself a control-plane operation and may be unavailable during a disaster.
rules.trigger: days_since_successful_restore_test>restore_test_interval_days OR restore_test_count=0 OR backup_account_id=source_account_id OR vault_lock_or_object_lock=false
rules.exception: Data fully and demonstrably reproducible from another system of record - then the reproduction is the thing that must be tested. Same-Region backup is normal and often required by residency law; Region separation is a DR-tier decision, not a backup requirement, so do not fail a compliant single-Region workload on that alone. The 90-day interval is a convention; monthly or per-release is warranted where schemas change often.

rules.rule: IF an encrypted resource may ever be shared cross-account, restored in another account, or restored in another Region THEN it MUST use a customer managed key, and a cross-Region recovery path needs a MULTI-REGION key created as such (a single-Region key can never be converted). Separately, every customer managed key policy MUST retain a durable account principal with at least kms:PutKeyPolicy and kms:GetKeyPolicy.
rules.plain: Pick your own KMS key up front if you will ever share or restore elsewhere, and always keep a statement that lets your own account manage the key. AWS-managed keys can never be shared, and a key with no manageable principal is bricked.
rules.why: AWS managed key policies cannot be modified, so a snapshot encrypted with aws/rds cannot be shared at all - discovered during a DR test, after the data exists. KMS is the exception to normal resource policies: the key policy does not implicitly grant the owning account, and IAM policies are inert unless the key policy enables them. If the only named principal is a role you later delete, nobody can change the policy and every ciphertext under that key needs an AWS Support case.
rules.trigger: (encryption_key_type=aws_managed AND (cross_account_share_required=true OR dr_account_exists=true)) OR (key_manager=CUSTOMER AND NOT EXISTS statement WHERE principal=account_root AND action INCLUDES kms:PutKeyPolicy) OR (dr_region_exists=true AND key.multi_region=false)
rules.exception: Purely single-account, single-Region data with no cross-account DR plan may use AWS managed keys, which carry no monthly key charge - but they still incur KMS request charges. Deliberately locked-down keys may omit the root statement only with a documented, tested, multi-party recovery path and at least two durable principals holding kms:PutKeyPolicy. Exclude AWS managed keys (KeyManager=AWS) from the policy check; you cannot edit them. Customer managed key rotation is configurable between 90 and 2560 days with on-demand rotation available. Enable S3 Bucket Keys on SSE-KMS buckets: it cuts KMS request cost by up to about 99%.

rules.rule: IF the threat model includes credential compromise, insider threat or a bad automation THEN the DR and backup copy MUST live in a separate AWS account, not merely a separate Region.
rules.plain: If someone steals your admin credentials, a backup in the same account dies with the original. Keep DR copies in a different account.
rules.why: AWS recommends a different account for the highest level of resource and security isolation specifically where compromised credentials are part of the DR scenario, and notes cross-account backup protects against insider threat and account compromise. A same-account cross-Region backup protects against nothing an attacker with your credentials cannot also delete.
rules.trigger: backup_account_id=production_account_id AND threat_model INCLUDES credential_compromise
rules.exception: Small estates may accept same-account DR only if paired with S3 Object Lock or AWS Backup Vault Lock in compliance mode, which makes deletion impossible even for the account root.

rules.rule: IF a contractual or application RTO depends on an RDS Multi-AZ DB INSTANCE failover THEN treat the documented time as typical and unbounded above: AWS words it as typically completing within about 60 seconds (older wording 60-120s) and explicitly longer where large transactions or lengthy recovery are involved. Budget for the tail, require application connection retry, and require a documented failover TEST.
rules.plain: An RDS failover normally takes about a minute but has no guaranteed ceiling. Do not write a 30-second RTO against it, and make sure the app reconnects by itself.
rules.why: Failover flips the DB instance CNAME to the standby. Any client caching DNS or holding a dead connection stays broken long after the database is back - the database recovered in 90 seconds and the application was down for 30 minutes. Long-running uncommitted transactions extend recovery, so undersized instance classes make failover slower. Untested retry code is the norm and it does not work.
rules.trigger: engine=rds_multi_az_instance AND (app_connection_retry=false OR failover_test_count=0 OR target_rto_seconds<180)
rules.exception: RDS Multi-AZ DB clusters target roughly 35 seconds; Aurora is typically under 30 seconds and often around 10 seconds for a managed planned failover, because a replica is promoted on shared storage rather than a volume recovered. For sub-30-second targets use Aurora with a tier-0 reader plus a failover-aware driver (AWS JDBC wrapper), or absorb the window with a queue in front of writes.

rules.rule: IF failover depends on a DNS record change THEN record_ttl + negative_cache_ttl + resolver_slop + CLIENT resolver cache MUST all fit inside the RTO, AND connection lifetime MUST be bounded so long-lived pools re-resolve. For JVM clients assert networkaddress.cache.ttl <= 60 and networkaddress.cache.negative.ttl is small; fail only when it is explicitly -1, above 60, or a SecurityManager is installed with the value unset.
rules.plain: DNS failover is only as fast as the TTL plus whatever your clients cache, and a connection pool that never reconnects ignores DNS entirely.
rules.why: Teams set a 60-second RTO against a 3600-second TTL and find the gap during the incident. The dominant failure today is not TTL at all: an HTTP/2 or JDBC pool held open for hours never re-resolves regardless of TTL. A cached NXDOMAIN during endpoint re-creation causes the same outage as a stale A record - that is the Oct 2025 empty-record shape.
rules.trigger: failover_mechanism=dns AND (record_ttl_seconds+negative_ttl_seconds>rto_seconds OR max_connection_lifetime IS NULL OR (runtime=jvm AND (networkaddress.cache.ttl=-1 OR networkaddress.cache.ttl>60)))
rules.exception: Historical note, not a current default: modern JVMs with no SecurityManager installed default networkaddress.cache.ttl to 30 seconds, already inside the bound; infinite caching applied when a SecurityManager was present, and SecurityManager is deprecated for removal. Verify, do not assume in either direction. The RDS endpoint TTL is 5 seconds, so a long client outage after an RDS failover is a client-side caching defect. Mechanisms that do not need client re-resolution - Global Accelerator anycast, ARC routing controls, an in-Region load balancer swap behind a stable name, RDS Proxy - remove this class entirely.

rules.rule: IF cross-Region failover is fully automatic on health checks THEN flag it: a false alarm costs the full RTO and RPO loss for nothing. Automate every step and keep initiation manual. Within a Region, automatic failover SHOULD be automatic.
rules.plain: Automatic region failover can fire on a false alarm and lose data for nothing. Script every step, but let a human press the button.
rules.why: AWS advises caution with automatically initiated cross-Region failover precisely because recovery time and recovery point are greater than zero, so failing over when you did not need to incurs those losses anyway. Manually initiated, fully scripted failover is the documented middle ground. Inside a Region the penalty for being wrong is near zero, so ELB health checks, RDS Multi-AZ, ASG replacement and ARC zonal shift should all act automatically.
rules.trigger: failover_mode=automatic AND scope=cross_region AND (rto_seconds>0 OR rpo_seconds>0)
rules.exception: Workloads whose RPO is genuinely zero by construction (idempotent, replayable from an authoritative upstream log) can automate cross-Region initiation, because being wrong costs only capacity.

rules.rule: IF more than one Region accepts writes THEN declare exactly one write strategy - write-global, write-local or write-partitioned - AND declare the CONFLICT DETECTION mechanism. DynamoDB global tables reconcile with last-writer-wins and silently discard the loser.
rules.plain: If two regions both take writes, decide up front how conflicting writes are resolved. DynamoDB global tables simply keep the last write and throw the other away.
rules.why: AWS names three strategies and their consequences: Aurora Global Database suits write-global; DynamoDB global tables enable write-local with last-writer-wins; S3 bi-directional replication supports write-partitioned. Last-writer-wins silently loses data when the conflict is a financial balance rather than a profile field, and teams adopt it without knowing they chose it.
rules.trigger: region_count>1 AND all_regions_accept_writes=true AND (conflict_resolution_policy IS NULL OR conflict_detection_mechanism IS NULL)
rules.exception: Writes naturally partitioned by tenant or user ID have no conflicts - but the partitioning must be ENFORCED at the routing layer, not assumed. Write-local on monetary values additionally needs an idempotency key and a reconciliation ledger; that is an application obligation. Aurora Global Database gives roughly 1 second typical replication lag and up to 5 secondary Regions, with database RTO commonly quoted under a minute; application-side DNS and pool recovery add to that.

rules.rule: IF a DR plan exists THEN assert that the recovery path has been DEPLOYED from infrastructure as code INTO the DR Region within the chosen interval. IaC coverage percentage is a poor proxy: an undeployed template is an untested one.
rules.plain: Everything you need to rebuild must be code, and that code must have been run in the standby region recently. Coverage is not correctness.
rules.why: AWS states that without IaC it may be complex to restore in the recovery Region, increasing recovery time beyond the RTO. But templates never deployed there routinely fail on Region-unavailable services, hardcoded AZ names, AMI IDs and instance types that do not exist. Console-built resources also carry undocumented settings - security group rules, IAM trust policies, parameter groups - that nobody can reproduce under pressure.
rules.trigger: dr_plan_exists=true AND days_since_iac_deploy_into_dr_region>interval_days
rules.exception: Data is restored from backups, not IaC. Genuinely not IaC-reproducible on the recovery path and needing their own documented runbook: KMS key material and grants, ACM certificate validation, Route 53 zone delegation, third-party DNS and SaaS callbacks, the account itself, the deployment role and the state bucket.

rules.rule: IF data must survive an instance stop, hibernate, terminate, or an underlying host failure THEN it MUST NOT live only on instance store. Instance-store data survives only a guest OS reboot.
rules.plain: Local NVMe disks are wiped when the instance stops or the host dies. Only a plain reboot keeps the data.
rules.why: This is a documented physical property, not a risk. The fast host-attached NVMe looks like a free performance win until a routine stop/start for a cost or instance-type change silently returns an empty disk. The failure appears as data loss, not as an error, and it recurs because i- and d-family instances are chosen for speed and then quietly used as primary storage.
rules.trigger: storage=instance_store AND durability_required=true AND replication_factor<2
rules.exception: Correct and included in the instance price for caches, scratch, shuffle and spill directories, and for distributed systems that replicate across nodes themselves (Cassandra, Kafka with replication, Elasticsearch with replicas) where losing one node's disk is a routine handled event.

rules.rule: IF an in-memory store holds data whose loss would break the application THEN either it is not a cache - use MemoryDB, which is durable, multi-AZ and transaction-log backed - or it must be ElastiCache with Multi-AZ and automatic failover AND fully reconstructible from a durable store.
rules.plain: A cache can vanish. If losing it would break your app, use the durable in-memory database instead, or make sure it can be rebuilt.
rules.why: Cache nodes are replaced during maintenance, scaling and failure; a single-node cluster loses everything on replacement. Teams put carts and sessions in Redis with no replica and discover during a routine patch that cache miss means every user logged out. Redis/Valkey RDB and AOF persistence is not durability - AWS warns snapshot restore can lose data between snapshots.
rules.trigger: service=ElastiCache AND deployment!=serverless AND multi_az=false AND data_is_authoritative=true
rules.exception: A pure read-through cache where every miss is a slower correct answer needs no Multi-AZ if the origin can absorb a full cold-cache herd - verify that with a load test, not an assumption. ElastiCache Serverless is multi-AZ with automatic failover by default, so this check must not fire on it. Valkey is now the default and cheapest engine choice. Automatic failover still takes tens of seconds and the primary endpoint must be re-resolved, so the DNS-cache rule applies here too.

rules.rule: IF a TLS certificate is IMPORTED into ACM, email-validated, not associated with an integrated AWS service, or DNS-validated with its validation CNAME removed THEN automatic renewal will NOT happen. Alarm on the ACM DaysToExpiry metric and the ACM AWS Health event for every certificate, and separately schedule RDS/Aurora CA certificate rotation.
rules.plain: Watch every certificate's expiry, including the AWS-managed ones, because managed renewal can silently fail - and imported certificates are never auto-renewed at all.
rules.why: Certificate expiry is a self-inflicted, perfectly predictable, total outage, and it usually hits the one internal, mTLS or imported certificate nobody put in the renewal system. ACM auto-renewal is conditional on the validation CNAME still existing and the certificate being in use by an integrated service. The RDS regional CA bundle expires on a published schedule and rotation needs a client truststore update and, on some paths, a reboot.
rules.trigger: cert.imported=true OR cert.validation=EMAIL OR (cert.validation=DNS AND validation_cname_present=false) OR cert.in_use_by_integrated_service=false OR rds_ca_expiry_within_days<90
rules.exception: Short-lived mesh certificates (SPIFFE or Private CA under 24h) where rotation failure surfaces in minutes anyway. Express alarm thresholds as a FRACTION of validity rather than fixed days: public TLS certificate lifetimes are being reduced on a ratified schedule (about 200 days in 2026, 100 in 2027, 47 in 2029), so a fixed 45-day alarm will eventually sit inside a routine renewal window.

rules.rule: IF a component makes a remote call THEN it MUST set an explicit connect timeout and request timeout derived from the dependency's MEASURED p99.9, and MUST propagate a DEADLINE so downstream work is abandoned once the caller has given up. Default SDK and HTTP client timeouts (often 60s or none) are a defect.
rules.plain: Every call out must have a time limit taken from real measurements, and must tell the next service how long it has left.
rules.why: This is the control that makes the retry and backoff rules safe; without it they make things worse. Unbounded timeouts exhaust thread pools and connection pools, which is how one slow dependency cascades into a full outage, and downstream work that nobody is waiting for keeps consuming the capacity needed for recovery. A chain's p99 is the sum of each hop's tail, so per-hop budgets must add up to less than the caller's budget.
rules.trigger: remote_call AND (connect_timeout IS NULL OR request_timeout IS NULL OR request_timeout>caller_remaining_budget OR deadline_propagated=false)
rules.exception: Deliberately long-running streaming or websocket connections need a liveness mechanism (heartbeat, idle timeout) rather than a request timeout. Timeouts set from averages rather than the far tail cause spurious failures under normal load.

rules.rule: IF a client retries THEN it MUST have ALL of: exponential backoff with FULL JITTER (sleep = random(0, min(cap, base*2^attempt))); a finite total attempt budget; a circuit breaker; and a client-side rate limit or retry token bucket. Count retries across EVERY layer: with R retries per layer over L layers, worst-case amplification is (R+1)^L - three retries at four layers is 256x, not 81x.
rules.plain: When you retry, wait longer each time and add randomness, give up after a set number, and stop calling entirely once it is clearly down. Then add up every layer that retries, because they multiply.
rules.why: Retry storms are how a brief dependency blip becomes an hours-long outage: the dependency recovers, is immediately hit by the accumulated backlog from every client at once, and falls over again. The 7 Dec 2021 us-east-1 event was a congestive collapse in which a latent defect prevented clients from adequately backing off despite back-off having been in place and tested for years. Deterministic backoff is not a fix - it re-synchronises every client onto the same instants.
rules.trigger: retry_enabled=true AND (jitter=false OR max_total_attempts IS NULL OR circuit_breaker=false OR retry_token_bucket=false OR product_over_layers(attempts) > agreed_cap)
rules.exception: A single idempotent retry on a fast, local, low-fan-in call may skip the circuit breaker but still needs jitter. Never retry a non-idempotent operation without an idempotency key. Retryable 4xx are 408, 425 and 429 (and 409 for some idempotent APIs); everything else 4xx is not. Most AWS SDKs default to standard mode with max_attempts=3 - that default is usually one of the layers nobody counted.

rules.rule: IF an operation mutates state AND can be retried by any client, gateway or queue THEN it MUST accept a caller-supplied idempotency key and deduplicate SERVER-SIDE in a persistent store with a TTL longer than the maximum retry window.
rules.plain: Anything that changes data must be safe to run twice, because it will be. Have the caller send a unique key and ignore repeats, and check it on the server.
rules.why: At scale duplicate delivery is a certainty, not an edge case: SQS standard queues are explicitly at-least-once, Lambda event sources redeliver, and a timed-out request may already have succeeded. Without idempotency, retries double-charge customers and double-ship orders. Server-side deduplication is required because a client-computed result is never trustworthy.
rules.trigger: operation.mutates_state=true AND (idempotency_key_supported=false OR dedup_store=client_side OR dedup_ttl<max_retry_window)
rules.exception: Naturally idempotent operations (setting a field to an absolute value, adding to a set) need no key; counters, appends and payments always do. SQS FIFO content-based deduplication covers a 5-minute window only, which is shorter than many retry windows.

rules.rule: IF an SQS queue, SNS subscription, EventBridge rule target or asynchronous Lambda invocation exists THEN it MUST have a failure path AND an alarm on that path's depth with treatMissingData set to notBreaching for emptiness but a real alarm on >0. For Lambda async use ON-FAILURE DESTINATIONS (SQS, SNS, EventBridge or Lambda), which preserve the full invocation record including the error; the legacy DeadLetterConfig loses that context. EventBridge targets also need an explicit retry policy.
rules.plain: Every queue and async trigger needs a place for messages that keep failing, and somebody must be told when messages land there. A dead-letter queue nobody watches is a silent data-loss bin.
rules.why: Without a failure path the message is dropped after maxReceiveCount with no record. With one but no alarm, the data is preserved and still silently lost - teams find hundreds of thousands of messages months later. The DLQ's own retention clock bounds your recovery window: SQS retention defaults to 4 days and maxes at 14.
rules.trigger: async_target_exists AND (failure_destination_or_dlq=false OR dlq_depth_alarm=false OR (target=eventbridge AND retry_policy IS NULL) OR dlq.encryption != source.encryption)
rules.exception: Streams where replay from the source is authoritative (Kinesis, DynamoDB Streams with a retained iterator) may omit a DLQ but still need a failure destination and an iterator-age alarm. An encrypted source queue with an unencrypted DLQ is an audit finding this check must catch.

rules.rule: IF a service calls a dependency THEN classify it as critical (fail the request) or non-critical (degrade: serve stale, omit the feature, queue for later) BEFORE the incident, and TEST the degraded path with the dependency forcibly failed. Separately, the service MUST shed excess work fast (429 with Retry-After) rather than queue it, prioritise by request class, and reserve capacity for health checks and control operations.
rules.plain: For every external thing you call, decide in advance whether you fail or carry on without it - then actually test carrying on. And when you are over capacity, say no quickly instead of getting slow.
rules.why: Degradation code is the least-executed code in the system: fallbacks that call the failed dependency, caches never populated, timeouts longer than the caller's own. A server that accepts everything and slows down converts a capacity problem into a total outage, because every caller then times out and retries - which is the retry rule's amplification loop with the server as the trigger. Classification also exposes that the non-critical recommendation service is in the synchronous checkout path.
rules.trigger: dependency_count>0 AND (criticality_classified=false OR degradation_path_tested=false OR admission_control=false)
rules.exception: Dependencies that ARE the request (the primary database of a CRUD service) have nothing to degrade to; the honest answer is to fail fast with a clear error rather than invent a fallback.

rules.rule: IF cache entries share a TTL, or a deploy, flush or node replacement can empty the cache, THEN the origin will see its true load for the first time. Mitigate with per-key TTL jitter, request coalescing (single flight, including on MISSES of absent keys), serve-stale-while-revalidate, and jitter on every scheduled job - use the EventBridge Scheduler flexible time window rather than a fixed minute.
rules.plain: If lots of cached items expire at the same second, everything asks the database at once and it falls over. Spread out expiry, let only one request refresh each item, and never schedule fleet-wide work at exactly the top of the hour.
rules.why: A cache with a 99% hit rate hides the fact that the origin cannot serve 100% of traffic. Cold-cache capacity, not warm-cache capacity, is the real capacity number. A single-flight guard keyed on value presence is bypassed by a stampede on a key that does not exist, and an ElastiCache node replacement empties one shard and sends its share of traffic straight to the origin.
rules.trigger: cache_ttl_jitter=false OR single_flight=false OR negative_cache_absent=true OR (schedule.minute_is_fixed_literal AND jitter_window_seconds=0)
rules.exception: Very small caches over an origin that can genuinely serve full traffic do not need this - verify by actually flushing the cache under load test rather than assuming.

rules.rule: IF work is not needed in the user's response AND peak_arrival_rate/sustained_capacity > 2 THEN put a queue between producer and consumer and scale consumers on ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage (which reflects SLA breach directly) rather than on queue depth.
rules.plain: If work does not have to finish before you reply to the user, queue it. Then you buy enough machines for the average, not for the worst minute of the day.
rules.why: A queue converts a capacity problem into a latency problem, which is far cheaper, and it absorbs downstream failure because consumers can be down while the queue holds. Queue depth says nothing about throughput; age of the oldest message says exactly how far behind the SLA you are.
rules.trigger: peak_rps/sustained_capacity_rps>2 AND work_is_deferrable=true AND queue_absent=true
rules.exception: Never queue work whose result the caller must see (payment authorisation, login). A queue without a failure destination and a consumer-lag alarm is a silent data-loss machine, not a buffer, and the consumer's timeout must be shorter than the queue's visibility timeout or you get duplicate processing.

rules.rule: IF a user-facing request path makes N synchronous calls each with availability A AND those failures are INDEPENDENT THEN path availability is approximately A^N and latency is the SUM of tail latencies. Where hops cross Regions, accounts or third parties, break the chain with async events, caching or data co-location, and give every hop a propagated deadline.
rules.plain: Every service you must call before answering multiplies your chance of failure and adds its slowest moments to yours.
rules.why: Five services at 99.9% each give 99.5% combined, about 3.6 hours of downtime a month, and the chain's p99 is driven by each hop's p99 rather than its average. The independence assumption is usually false: shared AZ, shared dependency, shared deploy pipeline and shared retry storms correlate the hops, so real availability is worse than A^N exactly during the events that matter.
rules.trigger: request_path.user_facing=true AND request_path.synchronous_hops>hop_budget AND (deadline_propagated=false OR fallback_absent=true)
rules.exception: Chains of local in-VPC single-digit-millisecond calls with tight timeouts and fallbacks are acceptable. Any fixed hop threshold (the commonly quoted N>3) is a convention: the real boundary depends on per-hop availability and whether each hop has a fallback.

rules.rule: IF several workloads share one Lambda account concurrency pool, one database connection pool, or one thread pool AND at least one is low-priority or untrusted THEN set an explicit per-workload cap: reserved concurrency for the functions that must not be starved, maximum concurrency on SQS event source mappings for the rest, separate RDS Proxy endpoints, separate ECS services and target groups.
rules.plain: Do not let one noisy job eat all the capacity everyone shares. Give the important workloads a guaranteed slice and cap the rest.
rules.why: Shared unbounded pools turn a local problem into a total outage: a backlog replay consumes the whole regional Lambda concurrency and throttles the customer-facing API sharing it; one tenant's slow query holds every database connection. Reserved concurrency is both a floor and a ceiling.
rules.trigger: shared_pool=true AND workload_priority_classes>1 AND per_workload_limit_set=false
rules.exception: Reserved concurrency SUBTRACTS from the account's unreserved pool and the unreserved pool can never fall below 100, so reserving on many functions is itself a way to cause the outage described. Budget the total before allocating, and prefer event-source-mapping maximum concurrency for the non-critical majority.

rules.rule: IF a Lambda writes to the same source that triggers it (S3 bucket, SQS queue, SNS topic, DynamoDB table with streams) THEN require a DISTINCT sink, reserved concurrency, a CloudWatch alarm on RecursiveInvocationsDropped and on invocation rate, and an AWS Budgets action.
rules.plain: Never let a function write back into the thing that triggers it, and always cap its concurrency.
rules.why: Lambda's recursive loop detection stops a chain after roughly 16 invocations of the same triggering event using the X-Ray lineage header and covers Lambda, SQS, SNS and S3 - but it is per-event-chain, not a spend cap, and it does not catch a fan-out loop where each invocation creates NEW events. Reserved concurrency is the only hard ceiling on blast radius, and the bill is the failure mode: unbounded fan-out bills faster than any daily budget alert can fire.
rules.trigger: (lambda.write_targets INTERSECT lambda.event_sources) != empty OR (lambda.reserved_concurrency IS NULL AND lambda.event_source IN (s3,sns,sqs,dynamodb_streams))
rules.exception: Intentional recursion (paging through work, step-wise processing) can opt out of loop detection per account via Support; the concurrency cap and the alarm still apply.

rules.rule: IF a single unit of work can exceed 900 seconds THEN Lambda is the wrong primitive: decompose with Step Functions, or use ECS/Fargate or AWS Batch.
rules.plain: A standard Lambda is killed at 15 minutes, no exceptions. If a job might take longer, do not put it in Lambda.
rules.why: The 900-second function timeout is a hard, non-increasable quota. Workloads that pass today on average data volumes fail permanently the day input size grows, and the failure mode is a mid-transaction kill with partial writes.
rules.trigger: service=Lambda AND (p99_duration_seconds*3>900 OR input_size_unbounded=true)
rules.exception: Lambda Managed Instances functions invoked asynchronously or through an event source mapping (excluding Amazon MQ and DocumentDB) allow up to 5,400 seconds. Synchronous invocation behind API Gateway is capped far lower by the gateway's own integration timeout regardless.

rules.rule: IF a synchronous request or response payload exceeds 6 MB (asynchronous: 1 MB) THEN do not push it through the Invoke path: write to S3 and return a presigned URL. IF the function writes files THEN size /tmp explicitly: 512 MB by default, configurable to 10,240 MB and billed separately above 512 MB.
rules.plain: Lambda takes at most 6 MB in or out at a time synchronously, and 1 MB for async. Bigger payloads go to S3. Scratch space is 512 MB unless you raise it.
rules.why: Exceeding the payload quota fails the invocation outright and is a frequent cause of works-on-small-test-files, breaks-on-real-data. Be precise about the error: the Invoke API returns RequestEntityTooLargeException (HTTP 413) for an oversize REQUEST, but an oversize RESPONSE surfaces as a function-level error, not a 413 to the caller - which matters if you alarm on status code.
rules.trigger: service=Lambda AND ((invocation_type=sync AND max(request_payload_mb,response_payload_mb)>6) OR (invocation_type=async AND request_payload_mb>1) OR (writes_tmp=true AND ephemeral_storage_mb=512 AND max_file_mb>400))
rules.exception: Response streaming may exceed 6 MB but carries its own maximum response size quota of 20 MB, which IS adjustable through Service Quotas, and is throttled past the first 6 MB. Streaming is not uncapped - a design that streams 500 MB fails.

rules.rule: In Lambda, CPU is allocated in proportion to configured memory: one full vCPU arrives at 1,769 MB and allocation keeps rising to roughly 6 vCPUs at the 10,240 MB maximum (128 MB minimum). Do NOT size to observed memory usage. Run AWS Lambda Power Tuning and pick the measured cost-and-latency optimum.
rules.plain: In Lambda the memory slider is also the CPU slider. Measure with Power Tuning instead of guessing; a slow function is sometimes cheaper at higher memory.
rules.why: Billing is GB-seconds, so on a CPU-bound function doubling memory can halve duration and leave the bill flat or lower while cutting latency. Sizing to observed memory - the instinct from EC2 - is the wrong optimisation. Setting 1,769 MB is not a target in itself: below it CPU still scales continuously, and a multi-threaded CPU-bound function should often go well past it.
rules.trigger: runtime=lambda AND (power_tuning_run=false) AND (p95_duration_ms>target_latency_ms OR memory_sized_from_observed_usage=true)
rules.exception: Single-threaded runtimes gain nothing past 1,769 MB, which is the actual reason that number matters. I/O-bound functions that wait on a network call gain nothing from extra CPU and should be sized down. The claim that more memory usually lowers total cost is workload-dependent, not a rule.

rules.rule: Compute required concurrency as peak_rps * avg_duration_seconds and compare it with the ACCOUNT concurrency quota (default 1,000, adjustable into the tens of thousands, lower on new accounts) AND with what the upstream can admit (API Gateway default 10,000 rps steady with a 5,000 burst, a soft quota). Request the increase before launch. Also check the SUM of reserved concurrency across functions against the pool.
rules.plain: Work out how many Lambdas run at once - requests per second times how long each takes - then check that number against your account limit and against what the front door will let in. Ask for more before launch day.
rules.why: The upstream can admit far more traffic than the downstream can serve, and the resulting throttles look like random 429s and 502s under load. Concurrency is not requests: a 500 ms function needs 500 concurrent at 1,000 rps, a 2-second function needs 2,000. The account pool is shared, so one runaway consumer throttles every other function in the Region.
rules.trigger: service=Lambda AND (peak_rps*avg_duration_seconds > account_concurrency_quota OR sum(reserved_concurrency) > account_concurrency_quota-100)
rules.exception: Even after a quota increase, a per-function scaling limit of 1,000 new execution environments every 10 seconds rate-limits a vertical spike; provisioned concurrency is the fix there, not a quota ticket. Reserved concurrency subtracts from the shared pool and the unreserved pool can never drop below 100, so blanket reservation is itself a cause of the outage it is meant to prevent.

rules.rule: IF Lambda functions are VPC-attached THEN count Hyperplane ENIs against the per-VPC ENI quota (default 3,000, shared with EFS and other services, adjustable) AND assert the subnets have IP headroom for peak. Consolidate functions onto fewer unique subnet-plus-security-group combinations, because ENIs are shared per combination.
rules.plain: Lambda functions inside a VPC share network cards from a per-VPC pool and consume subnet IP addresses. Run out of either and functions stop starting.
rules.why: Exhaustion surfaces as EC2ThrottledException or init failures that look like a code bug, and the blast radius is every VPC-attached function in that VPC, not just the one that grew. Scaling a VPC-attached function into a /28 subnet fails in a way that looks like a cold-start problem.
rules.trigger: lambda_vpc_attached=true AND (projected_eni_count > 0.8*eni_quota OR subnet_free_ips < projected_peak_ips)
rules.exception: Hyperplane ENIs are shared across functions with the same subnet-and-security-group combination, so consolidating combinations dramatically reduces ENI count. The 3,000 figure is a per-VPC default that can be raised; it is not a hard ceiling.

rules.rule: IF Lambda is user-facing AND the p99 latency budget is tight AND (runtime IN (Java,.NET) OR measured p99 InitDuration exceeds the budget) THEN use SnapStart (available for Java, Python and .NET) or provisioned concurrency, or move to an always-warm container service.
rules.plain: Cold starts only matter when a human is waiting and the runtime is slow to boot. Measure init time rather than guessing from package size.
rules.why: Cold-start cost is dominated by runtime init and the dependency tree. For async or batch work an extra second is invisible, so provisioned concurrency there is pure waste. Blanket beliefs that Lambda is slow cause both over- and under-engineering.
rules.trigger: service=Lambda AND exposure=user_facing AND p99_init_duration_ms>latency_budget_ms
rules.exception: VPC attachment is NO LONGER a meaningful cold-start signal: since the 2019 Hyperplane ENI rework the added latency is in the low tens of milliseconds, and treating VPC-attached as a trigger sells provisioned concurrency nobody needs. Package size in MB is a poor proxy - 50 MB is the direct-upload zip limit, not a cold-start threshold. Node and Python functions under about 10 MB typically cold-start well under 300 ms.

rules.rule: Choose between Lambda and a container by DUTY CYCLE and by computing both bills from real invocation counts, durations and memory - not from a heuristic. Lambda bills GB-ms with no idle charge but a per-GB-second premium; containers bill wall-clock at commodity rates.
rules.plain: Lambda wins when the thing is mostly asleep. A long-running, steadily busy service is cheaper on a container you keep running. Do the arithmetic with your own numbers.
rules.why: Any fixed threshold here is invented. Two things move the crossover in 2026 and must be in the comparison: Lambda is covered by Compute Savings Plans, which narrows the premium against Fargate considerably, and Lambda Managed Instances price long-running Lambda at EC2 rates. A large-memory function invoked constantly is expensive even at modest volume.
rules.trigger: compute_choice_pending AND cost_model_computed_from_measured_invocations=false
rules.exception: Operational cost is real on both sides and rarely appears in the comparison: Lambda removes OS patching entirely, containers do not. Do not use average CPU utilisation as the input for a service that has no instance to measure.

rules.rule: Container hosting is a THREE-way choice, not two: Fargate (no hosts, per-task rate), ECS on EC2 (cheapest per vCPU if you achieve high bin-packing density, you own patching and scaling), and ECS Managed Instances (EC2-rate compute with AWS-managed patching and scaling). Compare Fargate rate times task size against instance rate divided by achieved packing density, using CURRENT published rates for your Region.
rules.plain: Fargate costs more per vCPU but you run no servers. EC2 is cheaper only if you keep hosts genuinely full. ECS Managed Instances now gives EC2 rates without the patching work, which removes the usual argument for Fargate.
rules.why: EC2 bills the whole instance whether tasks fill it or not, so achieved density is the whole comparison. The old ops-burden argument that tipped the maths toward Fargate is largely obsolete since ECS Managed Instances became generally available. Any fixed percentage premium for Fargate varies by Region and by whether Compute Savings Plans or Fargate Spot apply.
rules.trigger: service IN (ECS,EKS) AND workload=steady_state AND rate_comparison_computed=false
rules.exception: Fargate does not support GPUs, privileged mode, placement constraints or Docker volume drivers - if the task needs any of those, EC2 is the only option regardless of cost. Fargate Spot changes the maths again for interruptible work.

rules.rule: IF a Fargate task requests a CPU and memory pair outside the published valid combinations THEN task registration fails. Valid: 0.25 vCPU with 0.5/1/2 GB; 0.5 vCPU with 1-4 GB; 1 vCPU with 2-8 GB; 2 vCPU with 4-16 GB; 4 vCPU with 8-30 GB; 8 vCPU with 16-60 GB; 16 vCPU with 32-120 GB.
rules.plain: Fargate only sells fixed CPU and memory combinations. You cannot ask for a little CPU and a lot of RAM.
rules.why: Memory-heavy, CPU-light workloads (JVM caches, in-memory analytics) are forced to buy CPU they do not need, which silently inverts the Fargate-versus-EC2 cost comparison. EC2 has memory-optimised families for exactly this shape.
rules.trigger: launch_type=FARGATE AND (cpu,memory) NOT IN valid_fargate_matrix
rules.exception: Windows containers on Fargate cannot go below 1 vCPU at all, and the 8 and 16 vCPU sizes require Linux platform version 1.4.0 or later.

rules.rule: IF the requirement is only to run containers AND you need neither multi-cloud or on-prem portability, nor the Kubernetes ecosystem (operators, CRDs, service mesh, GitOps controllers), nor a platform team to own it THEN choose ECS: EKS adds a cluster charge of $0.10 per cluster-hour (about $73/month, us-east-1) before a single pod runs, plus real operational load.
rules.plain: Kubernetes is worth it when you need its ecosystem, its portability, or you have a platform team. Otherwise ECS does the same job with less to learn and no cluster fee.
rules.why: The hidden cost has historically been upgrades, and the fee is per cluster so a fleet of clusters multiplies it. Two things have softened the operational argument since 2024: EKS Auto Mode removes much of the node-management burden, and clusters with a STANDARD upgrade policy are auto-upgraded by AWS.
rules.trigger: service=EKS AND k8s_ecosystem_required=false AND platform_ownership_named=false
rules.exception: EKS is genuinely justified for multi-cloud or on-prem portability, heavy CNCF ecosystem use, existing Helm or operator investment, and multi-tenant platform teams, where ECS's simpler model becomes the constraint. Headcount thresholds for this decision are conventions, not facts.

rules.rule: Audit the EKS cluster UPGRADE POLICY across the fleet. supportType=EXTENDED (the default) means that once a Kubernetes version passes its end-of-standard-support date the cluster is billed at $0.60 per cluster-hour instead of $0.10 - a 6x increase, about $438 versus $73 a month. supportType=STANDARD means AWS auto-upgrades at end of standard support and you NEVER incur the extended rate.
rules.plain: Let an EKS cluster fall behind and the cluster fee jumps six times over - unless you set the upgrade policy to STANDARD, in which case AWS upgrades it for you and you never pay the penalty.
rules.why: Extended support is billed automatically with no opt-in. A fleet of stale clusters turns this into six figures a year while also carrying unpatched control planes. The claim that there is no exception is false: the exception is a single API field, and setting it is the whole remediation.
rules.trigger: service=EKS AND cluster.upgrade_policy.supportType=EXTENDED AND deliberate_timeboxed_exception=false
rules.exception: A deliberate, time-boxed delay where a vendor workload has not certified the newer version - budget for it and set an end date. Note the trigger cannot be computed from upstream Kubernetes release dates: use the per-version end-of-standard-support dates in the EKS release calendar, which differ from upstream. Prices are us-east-1.

rules.rule: IF designing a new workload THEN do not select AWS App Runner: it is no longer open to new customers. Use ECS with Fargate (or ECS Express Mode) for the same container-to-URL simplicity.
rules.plain: App Runner is closed to new customers. Do not build on it. Use Fargate instead.
rules.why: Choosing a service that no longer accepts new customers means no new-account onboarding, a shrinking roadmap and a forced migration later. This is the fastest-changing fact in the compute set and memory gets it wrong.
rules.trigger: service=AppRunner AND account_is_new_to_service=true
rules.exception: Existing App Runner customers can continue as normal; there is no immediate forced shutdown, so a running service need not be migrated in a panic.

rules.rule: IF the workload is a queue of independent jobs that tolerate scheduling delay THEN use AWS Batch rather than a hand-rolled Auto Scaling group or a long-running ECS service: it does queue-depth scaling, job dependencies, retries and Spot interruption re-queue natively.
rules.plain: For a pile of independent jobs that can wait, AWS Batch is the right tool - it queues, scales to zero, and retries for you.
rules.why: Hand-rolled equivalents leak idle instances between job bursts, which is where the money goes. Job duration is not the deciding factor: jobs well under 900 seconds are perfectly reasonable on Batch when the queue is deep.
rules.trigger: workload=batch_queue AND latency_tolerance_minutes>1 AND orchestrator=hand_rolled
rules.exception: AWS Batch on Fargate removes the instance-launch latency, so the usual objection that Batch scheduling latency is too high applies only to Batch on EC2 or Spot. If jobs must start within seconds of arrival, keep a warm Fargate service or a small always-on pool.

rules.rule: IF the workload is Linux AND the runtime is interpreted or compilable for arm64 (Python, Node, Java, Go, .NET Core, Rust, most containers and mainstream open-source servers) AND no x86-only dependency exists THEN evaluate Graviton as the default and BENCHMARK it. AWS publishes up to 20% lower cost and up to 40% better price-performance; realised delta varies by family and workload.
rules.plain: Amazon's ARM chips are usually cheaper and often faster for normal web and API work. Use them by default - but measure, do not assume the headline number.
rules.why: Staying on x86 out of habit is a standing overpayment on the largest line item in most bills, and Graviton is available on EC2, Lambda, Fargate, RDS, ElastiCache and OpenSearch. But up-to figures are maxima: single-thread-heavy and memory-bandwidth-bound workloads can regress, and the migration has a real one-time cost in multi-arch images and CI that the pitch treats as zero.
rules.trigger: os=linux AND compute_arch=x86_64 AND x86_only_dependency=false AND benchmark_run=false
rules.exception: Windows Server does not run on Graviton at all - a harder blocker than binaries. Other real blockers in practice: Python wheels and Node native addons with no arm64 build, commercial APM/AV/database agents, CUDA and AVX-512-tuned toolchains, older .NET Framework, per-architecture licensing, and vendor images published only for amd64.

rules.rule: IF using Spot THEN ALL of: the workload must tolerate the whole pool disappearing and must drain or checkpoint within the two-minute interruption notice; allocation strategy MUST be price-capacity-optimized (never lowest-price); diversify across many instance types and all AZs, preferably with attribute-based instance selection; enable Capacity Rebalancing; and keep an On-Demand base capacity in a mixed-instances policy. Never run stateful primaries, quorum members or single-instance production services on Spot.
rules.plain: Spot is much cheaper but AWS can take the machine back with two minutes' warning. Only run work that can die and be retried, spread across many machine types, with some on-demand always underneath.
rules.why: Interruption is driven by AWS capacity needs, not your bid. A single-instance-type Spot request is a correlated failure: when that pool tightens the whole fleet goes at once. The two-minute notice is best-effort and is not guaranteed to be delivered at all; the separate EC2 rebalance recommendation has NO guaranteed lead time, so drain logic sized to a fixed pre-notice interval will be wrong.
rules.trigger: purchase_option=spot AND (allocation_strategy!=price-capacity-optimized OR capacity_rebalancing=false OR instance_type_diversity<4 OR on_demand_base_capacity=0 OR interruption_handler=absent OR workload_stateful=true)
rules.exception: Stop or hibernate interruption behaviour is only available for PERSISTENT Spot requests and is not available in the common Spot Fleet and ASG-managed configurations; a stopped Spot instance restarts only when capacity returns, which can be hours, so it is not a substitute for durability. Fargate Spot sends SIGTERM with a two-minute grace. The four-instance-type figure is a convention; attribute-based selection expresses the intent better.

rules.rule: IF configuring a Spot request THEN do not set a maximum price below On-Demand: it adds a second interruption cause for zero saving, because you never pay above the On-Demand rate anyway.
rules.plain: Leave the Spot max price blank. Setting one only gets you interrupted more often.
rules.why: With a max price set you are interrupted both for capacity AND whenever the Spot price crosses your ceiling - two interruption causes instead of one, with no price benefit.
rules.trigger: purchase_option=spot AND max_price_set=true
rules.exception: Defensible only where you have a hard per-hour budget ceiling and genuinely prefer no instance to an expensive one.

rules.rule: IF an EC2 T-family instance carries sustained load above its baseline CPU percentage THEN it is running on CPU credits: in standard mode it throttles to baseline when credits exhaust, and in unlimited mode it silently bills surplus credits per vCPU-hour. Alarm on CPUCreditBalance and CPUSurplusCreditBalance, or move to a fixed-performance family.
rules.plain: T-family instances sprint on credits. When the credits run out the machine either crawls or quietly starts costing more than the bigger instance you avoided.
rules.why: This is the same burst-credit failure shape as gp2 volumes and EFS Bursting throughput, and it is the one most often left unmonitored: fine in testing on a small dataset, collapses or overspends under sustained production load, and the metric that shows it is rarely alarmed. Unlimited mode converts an availability incident into an invisible cost incident.
rules.trigger: instance_family LIKE t% AND (sustained_cpu_pct>baseline_cpu_pct) AND (credit_balance_alarm=false OR surplus_credit_alarm=false)
rules.exception: Genuinely spiky, low-average workloads (small dev boxes, bastions, low-traffic APIs) are exactly what T-family is for; the rule is about SUSTAINED load, not peaks.

rules.rule: IF an EBS volume is gp2 THEN migrate it to gp3 with a live Elastic Volumes modification: gp3 is about 20% cheaper per GiB and gives a flat 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s baseline at ANY size with no burst credits, provisionable to 80,000 IOPS and 2,000 MiB/s independently of capacity, with a 64 TiB maximum against gp2's 16 TiB. gp2 below 1,000 GiB runs on burst credits and collapses to its 3 IOPS/GiB baseline when they exhaust.
rules.plain: gp3 is cheaper and faster than gp2 for almost every volume and you can switch without downtime. Small gp2 volumes sprint to 3,000 IOPS and then fall off a cliff.
rules.why: gp2 ties IOPS to size (3 IOPS per GiB, minimum 100, capped at 16,000 IOPS at 5,334 GiB) and relies on credits that silently exhaust - the classic the-database-was-fine-for-three-weeks-then-fell-over-at-2am incident, because BurstBalance hitting zero looks like an application hang. gp3 decouples the two so you stop over-provisioning capacity purely to buy IOPS.
rules.trigger: service=EBS AND (volume_type=gp2) AND NOT (1000<=size_gib<=5334 AND required_iops>3000)
rules.exception: Between 1,000 GiB and about 5,334 GiB a gp2 volume already gets more than gp3's free 3,000 IOPS baseline, so the equivalent gp3 needs PAID extra IOPS - check the per-volume maths before assuming a saving. The post-exhaustion baseline is not universally 100 IOPS: that applies only at 33 GiB or smaller; a 500 GiB gp2 falls to 1,500 IOPS. gp3 throughput above 125 MiB/s costs extra, and each volume modification has a 6-hour cooldown. Alarm on BurstBalance below 20% for 5 minutes.

rules.rule: IF required single-volume IOPS <= 80,000 AND throughput <= 2,000 MiB/s AND sub-millisecond latency is not a stated requirement THEN use gp3, not io2. Reserve io2 Block Express for beyond those figures, for Multi-Attach with NVMe reservations, or for the 99.999% durability requirement.
rules.plain: gp3 covers almost everything. Only pay for io2 when you genuinely need more IOPS or throughput than one gp3 volume can give, shared attach, or five-nines durability.
rules.why: io2 provisioned IOPS are billed per IOPS on top of storage and can multiply a volume's cost several times. io2 is bought reflexively for the production database when gp3 would meet the measured need.
rules.trigger: volume_type=io2 AND provisioned_iops<=80000 AND multi_attach=false AND durability_requirement!=99.999
rules.exception: The 80,000 IOPS ceiling is PER VOLUME, so RAID-0 across several gp3 volumes beats a single io2 on cost for many throughput-bound cases - the real fork is single-volume IOPS requirement, not total IOPS. io2 Block Express reaches 256,000 IOPS and 4,000 MiB/s on supported Nitro instances. AWS documents io2 Block Express as sub-millisecond; a 500-microsecond figure is not a published spec and latency triggers are not machine-checkable anyway.

rules.rule: IF the AGGREGATE provisioned IOPS or throughput across ALL volumes attached to an instance exceeds that instance type's EBS bandwidth THEN the instance, not the volume, is the bottleneck. Size the instance's EBS bandwidth first, and compare against its SUSTAINED figure, not its burst figure.
rules.plain: Buying more disk IOPS does nothing if the server cannot push that much traffic to disk - and the headline number in the table is often a burst number.
rules.why: Paying for tens of thousands of provisioned IOPS on an instance capped far below is money burned every hour with no performance gain, and it hides the real fix (a bigger or newer instance family). EBS bandwidth is shared across all attached volumes, so a per-volume comparison misses the common six-volumes-on-one-instance case. Most smaller instance sizes deliver their headline EBS bandwidth only in burst.
rules.trigger: sum(provisioned_iops_all_volumes)>instance_sustained_ebs_iops OR sum(provisioned_throughput_mibs)>instance_sustained_ebs_throughput
rules.exception: Non-Nitro instance types cap at 32,000 achieved IOPS even when attached to a volume provisioned for more, so on older families the ceiling is lower again.

rules.rule: IF EBS snapshots exist without a lifecycle policy (Data Lifecycle Manager or AWS Backup) THEN snapshot count grows unbounded, and deleting a source volume does NOT delete its snapshots. Separately, a volume restored from a snapshot is lazy-loaded from S3 and is SLOW on first touch unless Fast Snapshot Restore is enabled - which is billed per snapshot per AZ per hour.
