rules.plain: Give every snapshot schedule an expiry and check the oldest one. And know that a restored volume is slow until every block has been read once, which repeatedly turns a successful restore into a failed recovery deadline.
rules.why: Snapshots are incremental so the first ones look cheap, and orphaned snapshots of deleted volumes are the most common unnoticed storage line. The restore-speed trap is worse: the restore drill succeeds, the RTO measurement does not account for lazy loading, and the real recovery is far slower than the test suggested.
rules.trigger: service=EBS AND (lifecycle_policy_absent=true OR (snapshot.source_volume_exists=false AND snapshot.age_days>retention_days)) OR (restore_on_recovery_path=true AND fast_snapshot_restore=false AND rto_measured_with_lazy_load=false)
rules.exception: A snapshot that is the only remaining copy of a decommissioned system may be the cheapest possible archive - move it to the EBS Snapshots Archive tier (90-day minimum) rather than deleting it. Fast Snapshot Restore is expensive to leave on permanently; enable it as part of the recovery runbook, not as a default.

rules.rule: IF more than one instance or task must read and write the same POSIX filesystem concurrently THEN use EFS (or FSx); for a single writer needing a block device use EBS. On EFS, distinguish PERFORMANCE mode from THROUGHPUT mode: General Purpose performance mode caps at 35,000 read and 7,000 write IOPS regardless of throughput mode, while Bursting THROUGHPUT gives 50 MiB/s per TiB baseline bursting to 100 MiB/s per TiB. Elastic is the default throughput mode for new file systems.
rules.plain: EFS is for when many machines need the same folder at once. Do not use it as a general disk. And if an old file system is on Bursting, its speed depends on how much you store - switching to Elastic fixes throughput, not the IOPS ceiling.
rules.why: EFS is routinely used as a lazy shared drive for things that belong in S3 or on an EBS volume, at a multiple of the price. The Bursting failure has the same shape as gp2 credits: fine in test with a small dataset, starved in production, with BurstCreditBalance and PercentIOLimit rarely alarmed. Conflating the IOPS ceiling with the throughput mode leads to a switch that does not fix the symptom.
rules.trigger: (storage=EFS AND concurrent_writers<=1) OR (service=EFS AND throughput_mode=bursting AND size_tib<1 AND sustained_throughput=true) OR (service=EFS AND percent_io_limit_alarm=false)
rules.exception: With Elastic throughput and General Purpose performance mode, EFS now delivers as low as about 250 microseconds read latency for frequently-accessed data - sub-millisecond, not the older millisecond figures - so do not rule it out on stale latency numbers. EFS Infrequent Access and Archive classes with intelligent tiering change the price comparison materially for cold data. Windows/SMB needs FSx for Windows and HPC needs FSx for Lustre; EFS is NFS only. Throughput mode changes have a 24-hour cooldown. Per-client throughput caps at 500 MiB/s, or 1,500 MiB/s with the v2 client.

rules.rule: S3 cheaper classes bill MINIMUM DURATIONS and MINIMUM OBJECT SIZES. Duration: Standard-IA and One Zone-IA 30 days; Glacier Instant Retrieval and Glacier Flexible Retrieval 90 days; Deep Archive 180 days, with early deletion billed for the remainder. Object size: Standard-IA, One Zone-IA and Glacier Instant Retrieval bill a 128 KB minimum per object; Glacier Flexible Retrieval and Deep Archive add about 40 KB of index and metadata overhead per object. A transition that violates either INCREASES cost.
rules.plain: Cheap S3 classes charge you for a minimum number of days and round tiny files up. Moving short-lived or small files there costs more, not less.
rules.why: Lifecycle rules that chain Standard to IA to Glacier to Deep Archive within months can charge each minimum in turn, so the archive tier costs more than never tiering. For a bucket of 2 KB log objects the 128 KB floor multiplies billed bytes by up to 64x while appearing to be an optimisation. Per-object TRANSITION REQUEST charges are the highest of any class for the Glacier tiers and are often the dominant cost for small objects.
rules.trigger: ((storage_class IN (STANDARD_IA,ONEZONE_IA) AND expected_lifetime_days<30) OR (storage_class IN (GLACIER_IR,GLACIER) AND expected_lifetime_days<90) OR (storage_class=DEEP_ARCHIVE AND expected_lifetime_days<180) OR (storage_class IN (STANDARD_IA,ONEZONE_IA,GLACIER_IR) AND avg_object_size_kb<128))
rules.exception: None on the charges themselves. S3 Standard and S3 Express One Zone have no minimum billable object size and no minimum duration. S3 Lifecycle does not transition objects smaller than 128 KB to Glacier tiers unless you opt in. If retention is legally fixed at years, Deep Archive is obviously correct and the minimum is irrelevant.

rules.rule: IF the access pattern is unknown, changing or unpredictable THEN set S3 Intelligent-Tiering as the default class: no minimum duration, no retrieval fees, automatic transition to Infrequent Access at 30 days and Archive Instant Access at 90 days. It is SAFE for small-object buckets too.
rules.plain: If you do not know how often the data will be read, use Intelligent-Tiering. It moves objects to cheaper tiers on its own and never charges retrieval fees.
rules.why: Hand-written lifecycle rules encode an assumed access pattern and then rot, and a wrong one triggers minimum-duration and retrieval charges that dwarf the monitoring fee. Correcting a widespread myth: objects under 128 KB are NOT charged the monitoring and automation fee - AWS removed that charge in 2021. Such objects simply stay in the Frequent Access tier at Standard rates and never tier, so the cost of using Intelligent-Tiering on them is a missed saving, not a charge.
rules.trigger: access_pattern=unknown AND storage_class=STANDARD AND lifecycle_rules_encode_assumed_pattern=true
rules.exception: Where the access pattern IS known and stable (compliance archives read once a decade) an explicit lifecycle rule to Deep Archive is materially cheaper. The deeper Archive Access (90+ days) and Deep Archive Access (180+ days) tiers are OPT-IN per bucket and make objects asynchronously retrievable in minutes to hours, so enabling them changes availability semantics, not just price. The per-object monitoring fee still scales with object COUNT for objects at or above 128 KB - measure with S3 Storage Lens first.

rules.rule: Every S3 bucket needs FOUR lifecycle elements, not one: AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload (commonly 7 days); NoncurrentVersionExpiration on any versioned bucket; ExpiredObjectDeleteMarker cleanup; and, where access data supports it, a transition or Intelligent-Tiering configuration for cold data. An expiration rule alone does NOT reduce cost on a versioned bucket.
rules.plain: Failed big uploads leave invisible chunks you keep paying for. On a versioned bucket, deleting an object only adds a delete marker and the old versions bill forever. Fix all four or the bill does not move.
rules.why: Incomplete multipart parts do not appear in ListObjects, so the bucket looks small while the bill grows; ingest buckets accumulate terabytes of unreferenced parts over years. And the most common complaint after adding a lifecycle rule - the cost did not fall - is a versioned bucket where noncurrent versions and delete markers were never expired.
rules.trigger: service=S3 AND (lifecycle_abort_incomplete_mpu=absent OR (versioning=Enabled AND (noncurrent_version_expiration=absent OR expired_object_delete_marker=absent)))
rules.exception: Set the abort window longer than your longest legitimate upload; a 7-day abort would kill a genuine multi-day transfer over a slow link. Objects under a legal hold or Object Lock retention must not be expired. Per-object last-access time is NOT exposed in standard S3 metadata - you need S3 Storage Lens advanced metrics, S3 Inventory plus server access logs, or Intelligent-Tiering itself, so an age-based cold-tiering trigger is not directly machine-checkable.

rules.rule: IF data cannot be regenerated from another source THEN do not use S3 One Zone-IA or S3 Express One Zone: both store data in a SINGLE Availability Zone and are not resilient to the loss of that zone, unlike every other S3 class (3 or more AZs).
rules.plain: One Zone classes keep your data in one building. If that building is lost, so is the data.
rules.why: The eleven-nines durability figure quoted for One Zone-IA describes device durability WITHIN the zone, not resilience to losing the zone. The cheaper price is bought with correlated-failure risk that the durability number conceals.
rules.trigger: storage_class IN (ONEZONE_IA,EXPRESS_ONEZONE) AND data_is_recreatable=false
rules.exception: Correct for derived and reproducible data: thumbnails, transcoded media, build caches, secondary copies, and S3 Express One Zone as a deliberately co-located low-latency working set.

rules.rule: IF archived data is on a recovery path THEN size the RTO against retrieval time AND request throughput. Glacier Flexible Retrieval: Expedited 1-5 minutes, Standard 3-5 hours, Bulk 5-12 hours. Deep Archive: Standard up to 12 hours, Bulk up to 48 hours, with NO Expedited option. At scale: restore requests are capped around 1,000 TPS per account (excess returns ThrottlingException), restore throughput tops out at roughly 1-2 PB per day, and objects over 5 TB restore at up to about 300 MB/s. Use S3 Batch Operations, never per-object RestoreObject calls.
rules.plain: Deep Archive can take half a day to two days to get data back and has no fast option. A mass restore is also rate-limited, so millions of objects take days, not hours.
rules.why: Backups are archived to the cheapest class and the restore drill is never run FROM the archived tier, so the RTO is discovered during the real incident. DR plans size the restore by bytes and forget the per-request ceiling: a few hundred million small objects throttle long before bandwidth is the constraint, and a single 50 TB object alone can take up to 48 hours.
rules.trigger: purpose=disaster_recovery AND ((storage_class=DEEP_ARCHIVE AND rto_hours<12) OR (storage_class=GLACIER AND rto_hours<5 AND expedited_capacity_reserved=false) OR restore_object_count>10000000 OR restore_size_tb>100)
rules.exception: Glacier Instant Retrieval gives millisecond access at archive-tier storage prices with a 90-day minimum and a per-GB retrieval fee - the right class for archives that must be readable immediately but are touched about once a quarter. Increased restore limits can be requested from AWS Support in ADVANCE, which is the only way to beat the defaults.

rules.rule: S3 supports at least 3,500 PUT/COPY/POST/DELETE and 5,500 GET/HEAD requests per second PER PARTITIONED PREFIX. IF a workload concentrates traffic on one prefix THEN it will receive 503 SlowDown responses regardless of bucket size. Spread keys across prefixes and design the key layout for the request pattern, not for human readability.
rules.plain: S3 scales by prefix, not by bucket. Hammering one folder path gives you slow-down errors no matter how big the bucket is.
rules.why: This is the most common S3 scaling wall at production scale and it is invisible from the console: the bucket looks healthy, requests fail. S3 does repartition automatically over time, but the repartition lags a sudden hot-prefix workload, so the design must not rely on it. Date-prefixed keys (YYYY/MM/DD/) are the classic offender because every writer targets the same prefix at once.
rules.trigger: service=S3 AND (peak_put_rps_per_prefix>3500 OR peak_get_rps_per_prefix>5500) OR key_layout=monotonic_date_prefix
rules.exception: Retry with exponential backoff and jitter on 503 SlowDown is required regardless. For very high request rates on a co-located working set, S3 Express One Zone offers far higher per-directory request rates - at single-AZ durability, which the One Zone rule governs.

rules.rule: IF the application requires in-place PARTIAL WRITES, POSIX rename semantics, or full POSIX behaviour THEN S3 is the wrong store regardless of cost: use EBS (single writer), EFS (shared POSIX) or FSx. S3 has NO rename - only copy-then-delete - and that is the property that breaks ported code.
rules.plain: S3 stores whole objects and cannot rename anything cheaply. Software that expects a real filesystem needs EBS, EFS or FSx.
rules.why: S3-as-a-filesystem shims turn every small write into a full object rewrite and every directory listing into a paginated API sweep, producing terrible latency AND a request-count bill nobody predicted. Rename is the real killer: a directory rename becomes N copies plus N deletes, charged and non-atomic.
rules.trigger: storage=S3 AND (partial_writes_required=true OR posix_rename_required=true OR posix_semantics_required=true)
rules.exception: Be precise about what S3 CAN now do, or teams will move to EFS unnecessarily: S3 has supported conditional writes with If-None-Match and If-Match since 2024, which gives compare-and-swap coordination primitives, and Mountpoint for S3 now supports appends and partial overwrites in defined cases. Append-only and write-once-read-many patterns (logs, media, backups, data lake files) fit S3 perfectly.

rules.rule: A VPC primary IPv4 CIDR must be between /16 and /28 and an associated CIDR block's SIZE CAN NEVER BE CHANGED. Subnets cannot be resized either, and AWS reserves FIVE addresses in every IPv4 subnet, so usable = 2^(32-prefix) - 5, with /28 (11 usable) as the floor. Size from projected PEAK ENI and IP consumption, not from tidiness.
rules.plain: Pick your IP ranges as if permanent. You can never grow or shrink one. And AWS takes five addresses out of every subnet, so a /28 gives you eleven, not sixteen.
rules.why: Teams create a small CIDR to be tidy, run out when EKS pods, Fargate tasks, interface endpoints, NAT gateways and Lambda ENIs each consume real addresses, and find that exhaustion surfaces as opaque scheduling or scaling failures rather than an out-of-IPs error. Many ENIs consume more than one address, and with EKS prefix delegation a node reserves /28 prefixes at a time, so required addresses exceed required ENIs.
rules.trigger: projected_peak_ip_consumption > (2^(32-subnet_prefix)-5) OR vpc.total_usable_addresses < projected_peak_ip_consumption
rules.exception: The escape hatches are real and should be tried before a VPC rebuild: additional IPv4 CIDR associations (a per-VPC Service Quota with a DEFAULT of 5, raisable to 50 - the IPv6 equivalent is 5 and is NOT adjustable), secondary CIDRs drawn from the 100.64.0.0/10 CGNAT range for pod and ENI address space, EKS VPC CNI prefix delegation, and IPv6 or dual-stack subnets (which are /44 to /64 and do not use this formula). Note: BYOIP ranges get NO special treatment - the five reserved addresses apply to every IPv4 subnet.

rules.rule: IF a VPC has a NAT gateway AND sends traffic to S3 or DynamoDB in the SAME Region THEN add a Gateway VPC endpoint for that service: gateway endpoints have no hourly and no per-GB charge, while NAT bills a per-GB data-processing fee (about $0.045/GB in us-east-1, materially higher in several other Regions) on top of transfer.
rules.plain: Traffic to S3 and DynamoDB should use the free gateway endpoints, not the NAT gateway you pay per gigabyte for.
rules.why: S3 and DynamoDB are the only two services with free gateway endpoints, so backup, log and data-lake traffic through NAT is pure waste, and it is invisible because the bill says NAT Gateway, not S3. At 10 TB/month in us-east-1 that is roughly $450/month removed by a route-table entry.
rules.trigger: nat_gateway_count>0 AND same_region_s3_or_dynamodb_traffic_gb_month>0 AND gateway_endpoint_exists=false
rules.exception: Gateway endpoints are route-table based: they do NOT work from on-premises over Direct Connect or VPN, from a peered VPC, from a Transit Gateway attachment, or for cross-Region S3 - those need an interface endpoint (S3 has one, and it is paid) or NAT. Adding one injects a managed prefix list into every associated route table, which counts against the route-table route quota and can silently break egress inspection appliances or third-party S3 proxies. Gateway endpoint policies default to full access; scope them.

rules.rule: Compute the interface-endpoint breakeven as a FORMULA, not a constant: endpoint fixed cost is about $0.01 per endpoint-ENI hour per AZ (about $7.30/AZ/month) plus about $0.01/GB, against NAT at about $0.045/GB processing. When the NAT gateway is retained for other egress its hourly fee is sunk, so the saving is about $0.035/GB and breakeven is about 209 GB/month PER AZ - roughly 625 GB/month across three AZs.
rules.plain: PrivateLink endpoints cost about seven dollars per zone per month plus a penny a gig. Past a few hundred gigabytes a month per zone they beat NAT - but do the sum with your own zone count and Region prices.
rules.why: Teams add an endpoint for every service for security and end up with dozens of endpoint-ENIs costing hundreds a month to avoid a few GB of NAT traffic; or they delete endpoints that were saving money because they used a single-AZ constant. Interface endpoint per-GB pricing is also tiered, and if clients in one AZ use an endpoint ENI in another AZ, cross-AZ charges apply and can invert the answer - deploy an endpoint ENI in every AZ you have subnets in.
rules.trigger: nat_gateway_count>0 AND interface_endpoint_exists=false AND service_traffic_gb_month > (209 * endpoint_az_count)
rules.exception: Below breakeven, or where the service is accessed rarely and you already need NAT anyway, one shared NAT is cheaper. Where compliance requires that traffic never traverse a public AWS endpoint, or the subnet has no internet route at all, the endpoint is mandatory and cost is not the deciding factor. Some newer services are reachable ONLY by interface endpoint. Re-read the pricing pages per Region; the constants above are us-east-1.

rules.rule: IF private subnets exist in more than one AZ AND nat_gateway_count < private_subnet_az_count THEN each AZ without its own NAT gateway loses ALL outbound internet when the NAT's AZ fails, and its egress is charged as cross-AZ transfer. Deploy one NAT gateway per AZ with PER-AZ route tables.
rules.plain: One NAT gateway shared by three zones means one zone failure kills outbound internet for all of them, and you pay extra for the cross-zone traffic.
rules.why: A NAT gateway is a zonal resource, and traffic between it and an instance is free only within the same AZ. A single shared NAT converts a zonal failure into a total egress outage - the classic we-are-multi-AZ-but-everything-still-broke incident - and most teams do not know they have it because the single NAT was the module default. The mitigation requires per-AZ route tables, which many estates do not actually have.
rules.trigger: private_subnet_az_count>1 AND (nat_gateway_count<private_subnet_az_count OR route_tables_are_shared_across_az=true)
rules.exception: Dev, test and low-volume environments may accept the AZ-level egress outage IN WRITING; workloads whose egress is entirely to AWS services should use VPC endpoints and may need no NAT at all. Each extra gateway adds a fixed hourly fee (about $32.85/month in us-east-1, higher elsewhere). NAT gateways cannot be attached to a security group and their private IP cannot be changed. NAT INSTANCES are now a discouraged pattern - the AWS NAT instance AMI is deprecated - and they add a billed public IPv4 address.

rules.rule: A NAT gateway supports at most 55,000 simultaneous connections to EACH unique destination IP and port. IF a chatty fleet calls a single API endpoint through one NAT gateway THEN it will hit ErrorPortAllocation. Alarm on the ErrorPortAllocation CloudWatch metric and spread across per-AZ NAT gateways, or reach the destination through PrivateLink.
rules.plain: A NAT gateway can only hold 55,000 connections to any one destination address and port. A busy fleet calling one API will run out.
rules.why: This is the more common production NAT incident than AZ failure and it is entirely absent from most reviews. It argues for per-AZ NAT gateways independently of cost or availability, and it appears as intermittent connection failures to one destination while everything else works - which is diagnosed last.
rules.trigger: nat_gateway_count>0 AND (peak_concurrent_connections_per_destination>44000 OR error_port_allocation_alarm=false)
rules.exception: The limit is per unique destination IP and port, so a fleet talking to many destinations is far from it. Adding NAT gateways multiplies the ceiling only if traffic is actually distributed across them by per-AZ route tables.

rules.rule: IF a non-production VPC runs a NAT gateway that processes almost no data THEN the fixed hourly charge (about $32.85/month per gateway in us-east-1, $40-$68 in higher-cost Regions) is the whole bill. Prefer VPC endpoints for the handful of services actually called, or an egress-only internet gateway for IPv6, which has NO hourly and NO per-GB charge.
rules.plain: A NAT gateway costs about thirty-three dollars a month even if it moves nothing. In dev and test, replace it with endpoints or an IPv6 egress-only gateway.
rules.why: Partial hours bill as full hours, so three AZs across five non-prod accounts is hundreds of dollars a month for a few gigabytes of traffic. The cheapest answer is usually neither a NAT gateway nor a NAT instance but no NAT at all.
rules.trigger: nat_gateway_count>0 AND monthly_gb_processed_per_gateway<100 AND environment!=production
rules.exception: Do NOT apply this to production: the managed gateway's availability and scaling are worth the fixed fee, and a NAT instance is a single point of failure, an OS you must patch, and now also a billed public IPv4 address. A non-prod environment that is the staging gate for production must match production's egress path, or you are testing a different network.

rules.rule: Traffic crossing an AZ boundary within a Region is charged about $0.01/GB at the sender AND about $0.01/GB at the receiver, so one GB crossing a boundary costs about $0.02 in total. IF a chatty service pair, cache or mesh exchanges more than about 1 TB/month across AZs THEN evaluate zonal or topology-aware routing that prefers same-AZ targets while keeping capacity in every AZ.
rules.plain: Sending data between zones costs two cents a gigabyte because both ends are billed. It is invisible on the architecture diagram and very visible on the bill.
rules.why: Service meshes and client-side load balancers distribute evenly across AZs by default, which MAXIMISES cross-AZ traffic. A path whose client, load balancer and target sit in three different AZs can be charged on two separate AZ-crossing hops. Same-AZ private IP traffic within a Region is free.
rules.trigger: cross_az_gb_month>1000 AND topology_aware_routing=false
rules.exception: NEVER collapse to a single AZ to save this - the availability loss is worth far more than the transfer charge, and quorum systems (etcd, Kafka ISR, synchronous replication) MUST cross AZs. Significant carve-outs that change the answer: RDS Multi-AZ primary-to-standby replication is not charged; Aurora traffic between the writer and readers over the cluster volume is not charged; regional data transfer between an ALB or NLB and its targets is not separately charged; EFS and S3 same-Region access do not incur AZ transfer. Prices are us-east-1 and Region-specific.

rules.rule: Any AWS cost estimate MUST model six line items, not three: (1) compute time, (2) storage GB-month, (3) requests and I/O operations, (4) data transfer AND per-GB PROCESSING, (5) per-hour charges for provisioned-but-idle attachments (NAT gateways, endpoint ENIs, load balancer LCUs, public IPv4 addresses), and (6) control-plane and API charges (CloudWatch PutMetricData, KMS requests, S3 LIST/GET). An estimate missing 4, 5 or 6 is invalid.
rules.plain: AWS bills for more than machines and disks. The surprises are always the per-gigabyte processing fees, the hourly charges on idle attachments, and the API calls.
rules.why: These fees are not attached to any resource you consciously provisioned, so they are left at zero in a calculator built by picking instances - the AWS Pricing Calculator DOES have transfer fields, they simply default to zero. This is the most common source of a bill two to three times the forecast, and for small-object workloads the request count, not the bytes, dominates.
rules.trigger: activity=cost_estimate AND (data_transfer_modelled=false OR idle_hourly_attachments_modelled=false OR request_charges_modelled=false)
rules.exception: Wholly single-AZ, single-service workloads with no internet egress (a batch job reading and writing S3 in-Region through a gateway endpoint) can genuinely have near-zero transfer cost.

rules.rule: Inbound data transfer AT THE INTERNET GATEWAY is not charged; outbound to the internet is charged above a 100 GB/month allowance aggregated account-wide across services and Regions (excluding China and GovCloud), on a tiered rate starting around $0.09/GB in us-east-1 and falling with volume. CloudFront has its OWN separate 1 TB/month allowance and its own rates. Design so bulk data is pulled INTO AWS and only summaries leave.
rules.plain: Uploading to AWS over the internet is free. Downloading out is not, past the first 100 GB a month. Keep the big data inside and send out only small results.
rules.why: Egress is the deliberate lock-in price: a system that ships raw data out to be processed elsewhere pays per GB forever. Critically, INBOUND IS NOT UNIVERSALLY FREE - it is free only at the internet gateway boundary. Inbound through a NAT gateway is charged per-GB processing, inbound through an ALB or NLB consumes LCUs, and inbound to an interface endpoint is charged per GB. Treating inbound as zero is how a NAT-heavy ingest pipeline surprises everyone.
rules.trigger: (direction=egress_to_internet AND monthly_gb>100 AND cdn_offload=false) OR (direction=ingress AND path_includes IN (nat_gateway,interface_endpoint,elb) AND processing_cost_modelled=false)
rules.exception: Inter-Region transfer is materially more expensive than cross-AZ and is a first-order architectural finding at scale. Serving through CloudFront usually reduces both request load and per-GB egress cost, and origin fetches from AWS origins to CloudFront are not charged. All figures are us-east-1 list and must be re-read per Region.

rules.rule: Choose inter-VPC connectivity on COST and topology, not on connection count alone. VPC peering has no hourly attachment charge and no per-GB processing but is NOT transitive, so any-to-any needs n(n-1)/2 connections and per-VPC routes. Transit Gateway turns that into O(n) attachments with segmentation route tables, at roughly $0.05 per attachment-hour (about $36/month each) PLUS about $0.02/GB processing, supporting 5,000 attachments (adjustable) and up to 100 Gbps each direction per VPC attachment per AZ. AWS Cloud WAN is the option above a multi-Region, multi-segment estate.
rules.plain: Two or three VPCs: peer them. Many VPCs needing any-to-any: use Transit Gateway, but know it charges per attachment and per gigabyte, so a high-volume pair may be cheaper left peered. Multi-region, multi-segment: look at Cloud WAN.
rules.why: Peering has no transitive routing, so route-table maintenance rather than connection count is what kills you. But TGW per-GB processing means a six-VPC estate with heavy inter-VPC traffic can cost dramatically more on TGW than on peering, and peering scales further than usually assumed (125 active peering connections per VPC, adjustable).
rules.trigger: vpc_count>=4 AND connectivity=any_to_any AND transit_gateway=false AND cloud_wan=false
rules.exception: A hub-and-spoke where only spoke-to-hub traffic is needed, and any high-volume two-VPC pair, should stay peered even inside a large TGW estate. Appliance mode must be enabled on the TGW attachment for stateful inspection or flows break asymmetrically across AZs. Gateway endpoints do not work over TGW.

rules.rule: IF two networks must exchange traffic AND their CIDR ranges OVERLAP, or a provider must expose exactly one service to many consumers without granting network reachability, THEN use PrivateLink (an endpoint service behind an NLB or GWLB), not peering or Transit Gateway.
rules.plain: If two networks use the same IP ranges they cannot be peered. PrivateLink still works, because the consumer only ever sees one endpoint address in their own subnet.
rules.why: Peering and Transit Gateway are routing-layer solutions and flatly refuse overlapping CIDRs - a real problem after acquisitions or when every team copied 10.0.0.0/16. PrivateLink is unidirectional and service-scoped: the consumer gets an ENI in their own subnet, so the provider's address space is irrelevant and the provider's VPC is never exposed.
rules.trigger: (cidr_overlap=true AND connectivity_required=true) OR (exposure_scope=single_service AND consumer_count>1)
rules.exception: For BIDIRECTIONAL, general, many-port connectivity across overlapping CIDRs the documented answer is NOT to re-IP: use a PRIVATE NAT GATEWAY performing source NAT into a non-overlapping secondary CIDR, routed over Transit Gateway - that is how most post-acquisition estates are joined. PrivateLink requires an NLB or GWLB so it is TCP/UDP only (no ICMP), and consumer-side endpoint ENIs consume IP addresses in the consumer's subnets. Cross-Region VPC endpoints for endpoint services have been available since late 2024, so the same-Region assumption no longer holds.

rules.rule: Pick the Route 53 routing policy from the GOAL: latency for lowest response time across AWS Regions; geolocation for jurisdictional control; geoproximity (with a bias dial, and the only policy supporting non-AWS endpoints by latitude/longitude); IP-based for known ISP CIDR-to-location mapping; failover with health checks for active/passive DR; weighted for canary or gradual shift; multivalue answer for client-side spreading with health filtering.
rules.plain: Latency routing for speed, geolocation when the law says where traffic may go, geoproximity when you must include your own data centre, failover for DR, weighted for gradual rollouts.
rules.why: Picking latency routing when you needed data residency silently sends EU users to us-east-1, and no monitor flags it. Latency routing only works for AWS Regions, so it cannot include an on-premises endpoint - that is what geoproximity is for.
rules.trigger: service=Route53 AND record_set_count>1 AND routing_policy NOT IN policy_for(goal)
rules.exception: Two traps. First, DNS IS NOT A COMPLIANCE BOUNDARY: geolocation resolves by the RESOLVER's location (or EDNS client subnet where sent), not the user's, so a VPN or a centralised corporate resolver routes wrong - residency must be enforced by an authorization check at the endpoint. Second, if a geolocation endpoint is unhealthy Route 53 falls back to the larger geographic region's record and then the default record, NOT to a sibling location; to fail over between locations you must nest a failover record set under each geolocation record.

rules.rule: Use security groups (stateful, allow-only, referenceable by security group id) as the primary control and leave network ACLs at default allow-all. Add a NACL ONLY for a subnet-wide DENY a security group cannot express - blackholing a hostile CIDR, or a regulator-mandated subnet boundary.
rules.plain: Security groups are the firewall you should actually use. NACLs are stateless and can only block whole subnets; most teams that touch them just break things.
rules.why: Security groups are stateful, so allowing inbound automatically permits the return traffic. NACLs are stateless, so you must also explicitly allow the ephemeral return range 1024-65535 outbound - and the classic failure is a half-configured NACL silently dropping return packets while the security group looks correct. Security groups cannot express DENY, which is the one genuine reason a NACL exists.
rules.trigger: resource=NetworkACL AND rules!=default_allow_all AND explicit_deny_requirement=false
rules.exception: A real deny requirement, or defence-in-depth on a DMZ subnet, is exactly what a NACL is for - provided the ephemeral range is opened outbound.

rules.rule: The ONLY non-adjustable wall is the PRODUCT: rules_per_security_group x security_groups_per_ENI must not exceed 1,000 per network interface. The components ARE adjustable: 60 inbound plus 60 outbound rules per group by default (raisable, e.g. to 250), and 5 security groups per ENI by default with a maximum of 16. Reference other security groups by id rather than enumerating CIDRs.
rules.plain: One network card can carry at most a thousand security group rules in total. The sixty-rule and five-group figures are just defaults you can raise. Point groups at other groups instead of listing addresses.
rules.why: Teams that list individual CIDRs hit the 60-rule wall and stack more groups until they hit the per-ENI wall, then conclude they need a redesign when a quota request would have done. Raising rules-per-group to 250 forces groups-per-ENI down to 4 because the 1,000 product binds. A security-group-to-security-group reference counts as ONE rule per protocol and port range regardless of fleet size, which is why it scales.
rules.trigger: (sg_rules_per_eni_total>1000) OR (sg_inbound_rules>60 AND quota_increase_not_requested) OR (sgs_per_eni>5 AND quota_increase_not_requested)
rules.exception: Prefix lists are the correct escape hatch for large static CIDR sets, BUT a rule referencing a prefix list counts as the prefix list's MAX ENTRIES, not as one rule - a 50-entry prefix list consumes 50 of your 60, which is how teams blow the limit while believing they solved it.

rules.rule: IF a security group allows 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0 on an administrative or database port (22, 3389, 3306, 5432, 6379, 27017, 9200, 1433) THEN FAIL. IF a data store has PubliclyAccessible=true or sits in a subnet with a route to an internet gateway THEN FAIL. Human access to instances goes through Systems Manager Session Manager or EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint, not an open port.
rules.plain: Nothing administrative and no database should be reachable from the internet. Put data stores in private subnets, allow only the application's security group, and reach instances through Session Manager.
rules.why: A public subnet is defined purely by having a 0.0.0.0/0 route to an internet gateway - nothing else - and a database there is one over-broad rule from being scanned and brute-forced. Session Manager needs no inbound port, is IAM-controlled and is logged to CloudTrail and S3, which a bastion with a key pair is not. Referencing the application's security group id rather than a CIDR keeps the rule correct as the fleet scales.
rules.trigger: (sg.ingress_cidr IN (0.0.0.0/0,::/0) AND port IN admin_or_db_ports) OR (resource IN (RDS,Aurora,DocumentDB,ElastiCache,Redshift,OpenSearch) AND (publicly_accessible=true OR subnet_has_igw_route=true)) OR (ssh_key_pairs_in_use=true AND session_manager=false)
rules.exception: 0.0.0.0/0 on 80 and 443 to an internet-facing load balancer is normal and must be recorded as intentional; note that exposure, not port number, is what matters - an unauthenticated admin endpoint on 443 is worse than 8080 behind an ALB. A deliberately isolated sandbox with synthetic data, allow-listed to a corporate egress range, is a defensible temporary exception. Developers needing laptop access is NOT an exception - that is what Session Manager port forwarding or a VPN is for.

rules.rule: IF access patterns cannot be enumerated in advance, OR the workload needs ad-hoc queries, joins, aggregations or range scans on non-key attributes, THEN DynamoDB is the wrong choice - use a relational engine. IF all access is known key-based lookup AND scale or latency demands are extreme THEN DynamoDB is correct.
rules.plain: DynamoDB is only good when you already know every question you will ask of the data. If people will want to slice it new ways later, use SQL.
rules.why: DynamoDB's data model is designed around the queries, not the entities, so a new query pattern needs a new index or a full backfill. The failure mode is not an error, it is a Scan: the application works in staging with a thousand items and burns thousands of dollars of read capacity and seconds of latency in production.
rules.trigger: service=DynamoDB AND (access_patterns_enumerated=false OR requires_adhoc_analytics=true)
rules.exception: A DynamoDB table with a stream into OpenSearch, S3 plus Athena, or a zero-ETL Redshift integration handles the we-also-need-search-and-analytics requirement without giving up DynamoDB's operational characteristics. PartiQL does NOT change this rule - it is SQL syntax over the same key-based engine.

rules.rule: IF entities are accessed TOGETHER in one request THEN co-locate them in one table under a shared partition key. IF entities have independent lifecycles, independent scaling profiles, different TTL, backup or encryption requirements, or different owning teams THEN use separate tables.
rules.plain: Put data in one table when you always fetch it together. Use separate tables when the data is unrelated, scales differently, or belongs to another team.
rules.why: Single-table design exists for exactly one reason: DynamoDB has no joins, so co-locating related items lets one Query return a whole object graph in one round trip. Applied dogmatically it produces a table where one hot entity type throttles unrelated ones and no team can reason about capacity, backups or TTL independently. Separate tables cost nothing extra in on-demand mode.
rules.trigger: service=DynamoDB AND table_count=1 AND entity_types_accessed_together=false
rules.exception: Microservice boundaries override this entirely: two services should never share one table regardless of access-pattern overlap, because the table becomes a shared database and an undeclared coupling.

rules.rule: A single partition key value is bounded at 3,000 read units/sec and 1,000 write units/sec and cannot span partitions, so it WILL throttle regardless of table capacity. Separately, on-demand tables have a default table-level maximum around 40,000 RCU and 40,000 WCU (adjustable) and on-demand scales to only DOUBLE the previous observed peak, so a genuine 10x spike throttles even with a perfectly distributed key. Use warm throughput or pre-warming before a known launch spike.
rules.plain: Any single partition key tops out at 3,000 reads and 1,000 writes a second. And the table itself only doubles from its previous busiest moment, so a sudden ten-times spike throttles anyway.
rules.why: This is the hot-partition incident and it looks impossible from the console - the table shows unused capacity while requests fail. Classic triggers: a status equals PENDING key, a per-day partition key on a high-volume event table, or one tenant far larger than the rest. Adaptive capacity helps unevenness ACROSS partitions but can never exceed the per-partition ceiling.
rules.trigger: service=DynamoDB AND ((max_rcu_per_partition_key>3000) OR (max_wcu_per_partition_key>1000) OR (mode=on_demand AND projected_peak > 2*previous_observed_peak AND warm_throughput_not_configured))
rules.exception: Read-hot keys (a leaderboard, a product page) are better solved with DAX or an ElastiCache layer than with write sharding, since sharding a read-hot key adds fan-out query cost - but DAX does not serve strongly consistent reads and is itself a cluster to operate. Write sharding (suffix, calculated suffix, time-bucketing) remains the only answer for write-hot keys. Burst capacity may absorb sub-second spikes but is also consumed by DynamoDB's background tasks and must never be designed around.

rules.rule: A DynamoDB item may not exceed 400 KB - the write fails with ValidationException. IF a table has ANY local secondary index THEN no single item collection (all items sharing one partition key, across the table and its LSIs) may exceed 10 GB. Instrument ReturnItemCollectionMetrics and alarm at about 8 GB, not at 10.
rules.plain: No single DynamoDB item may exceed 400 KB. And if you use a local secondary index, everything sharing one partition key must stay under 10 GB in total.
rules.why: Both limits are enforced at write time and both are discovered in production when one customer grows larger than the others. The 10 GB collection limit is the nastier one: it applies only when an LSI exists, LSIs can be created only at table creation and can never be deleted, so you inherit the cap permanently.
rules.trigger: service=DynamoDB AND (max_item_size_kb>400 OR (lsi_count>0 AND max_item_collection_gb>8))
rules.exception: The 10 GB collection limit does NOT apply to tables without LSIs, nor to global secondary indexes. Prefer a GSI over an LSI for this reason alone unless you specifically need strongly consistent reads on the index - the only capability an LSI has that a GSI does not. Oversized items: compress, split across sort keys, or store the blob in S3 and keep the key as an attribute.

rules.rule: IF the projected relational dataset exceeds 128 TiB THEN a single Aurora cluster is not the answer: the cluster volume grows in 10 GiB increments to a hard maximum of 128 TiB. Plan sharding, archival to S3, or a different store before you reach it.
rules.plain: One Aurora cluster tops out at 128 TiB. If you will exceed that, plan how to split the data now, not at 120 TiB.
rules.why: Storage auto-grows silently and costs almost nothing to start, so teams never think about the ceiling until writes fail. Splitting a 100 TiB relational database under production load is a multi-quarter project; deciding the shard key at 5 TiB is a design meeting.
rules.trigger: service=Aurora AND projected_storage_tib>128
rules.exception: Aurora storage shrinks dynamically when data is deleted, so a high-churn table may never approach the limit. Aurora Limitless Database (sharded) exists specifically to break this ceiling for PostgreSQL workloads.

rules.rule: Set BOTH bounds on Aurora Serverless v2 deliberately. Minimum: 0 ACU enables scale-to-zero with an auto-pause idle window configurable from 300 to 86,400 seconds (default 300); otherwise the minimum non-zero capacity is 0.5 ACU, in 0.5 ACU steps. Maximum: up to 256 ACUs, and a generous maximum means a single runaway query can bill at the ceiling for an extended period - max_capacity is the number that needs a guardrail.
rules.plain: Serverless v2 can scale to zero and stop charging for compute when nobody is connected, but waking takes time. The bigger risk is the upper bound: one bad query can run up to your maximum and stay there.
rules.why: Each ACU is roughly 2 GiB of memory plus matching CPU. Setting the minimum to 0 on a dev or test cluster removes the single largest line item in most non-production accounts; setting it to 0 on a user-facing cluster turns an idle period into a visible cold start. Serverless v2 scales UP fast and down slowly, which is what makes an unguarded maximum expensive.
rules.trigger: service=AuroraServerlessV2 AND ((environment!=production AND min_acu>0) OR max_acu_guardrail_absent=true)
rules.exception: For HA with scale-to-zero the reader's failover tier must be 0 or 1 so it tracks the writer's capacity; otherwise a paused reader is not a credible failover target. A writer with trickle activity never pauses, so min=0 buys nothing. On monitoring: the documented constraint is that Performance Insights and Enhanced Monitoring cannot collect while the instance is PAUSED, and AWS's guidance for retaining PI data is to avoid scaling to zero - there is no documented 2-ACU floor, and quoting one is false precision.

rules.rule: IF compute is Lambda or an autoscaling fleet whose concurrency can exceed the database's max_connections THEN put RDS Proxy in front. Size MaxConnectionsPercent as a percentage OF THE DATABASE'S max_connections (commonly 75-100% for a dedicated proxy), use MaxIdleConnectionsPercent to control the warm pool, and control CLIENT concurrency with Lambda reserved concurrency. Alarm on DatabaseConnections approaching MaxDatabaseConnectionsAllowed.
rules.plain: Lambda can start a thousand copies of itself, each opening its own database connection, and kill the database. RDS Proxy pools and reuses connections so that cannot happen.
rules.why: max_connections scales with instance memory, so a small instance may allow only a few hundred connections while Lambda concurrency defaults to 1,000 per Region. Without a proxy the failure is too-many-connections errors under exactly the traffic spike you scaled for. The proxy also holds connections across a failover, cutting observed failover impact. Note the parameter is relative to max_connections, NOT to client concurrency - guidance phrased as a percentage above observed peak is not executable.
rules.trigger: (compute=Lambda OR autoscaling=true) AND db_engine IN (RDS,Aurora) AND rds_proxy=false AND peak_client_concurrency>db_max_connections
rules.exception: The proxy PINS a client connection to a database connection when it sees session state it cannot safely reuse (temp tables, session variables, some prepared statements); a workload that pins constantly pays the cost and an extra hop with none of the multiplexing benefit - watch DatabaseConnectionsCurrentlySessionPinned. The proxy is billed per vCPU-hour of the underlying instance, adds a few milliseconds per call, needs a Secrets Manager secret plus same-VPC placement for IAM auth, and enforces a NON-CONFIGURABLE 24-hour maximum client connection lifetime, so app pools must expire sooner. For genuinely spiky Lambda workloads, Aurora Serverless v2 or the RDS Data API is often the cheaper answer.

rules.rule: Match the store to the dominant query. Graph traversal over highly connected data: Neptune (and decide between Neptune Database and Neptune Analytics). Analytical aggregation over columns at TB scale: S3 with Athena or Iceberg first, Redshift when sustained query volume justifies it, Aurora zero-ETL to Redshift to avoid a pipeline. Sub-millisecond key lookup: ElastiCache for cache, MemoryDB when the data must survive. Time-series metrics: Timestream for InfluxDB, Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus, or PostgreSQL with TimescaleDB. Document queries over open-ended structure: DocumentDB or Aurora PostgreSQL with JSONB. Known key-based access at extreme scale: DynamoDB.
rules.plain: Match the database to the question you ask most. Bending one general database into every shape works at demo scale and collapses at real scale.
rules.why: Each of these workloads has a data-layout requirement a row store cannot satisfy: analytics on an OLTP instance scans rows to read one column and competes with production for buffer cache - the classic the-reporting-query-took-the-site-down - and multi-hop graph traversal in SQL becomes recursive self-joins that degrade super-linearly with depth.
rules.trigger: (workload=analytics AND engine IN (RDS,Aurora) AND data_tb>1) OR (workload=graph_traversal AND hops>2 AND engine=relational) OR (workload=timeseries AND retention_tiering_required=true AND engine=relational) OR (workload=queue_or_session_state AND engine=ElastiCache)
rules.exception: Timestream for LiveAnalytics is CLOSED TO NEW CUSTOMERS, so do not recommend it - use the alternatives named above. Below roughly a few hundred GB, a read replica of your existing PostgreSQL (or zero-ETL) is far cheaper and simpler than standing up a new engine, and an extra service is an extra thing to patch, monitor, back up and staff. PostgreSQL with TimescaleDB or pgvector covers many special workloads well enough at small scale. On the document-store question specifically, DocumentDB Serverless now exists so the pay-for-instances-24x7 objection is weaker, and DocumentDB targets MongoDB 5.0 compatibility; choose DynamoDB when access patterns are known and scale or latency are extreme, and a document engine when queries over document STRUCTURE are genuinely open-ended. ElastiCache is not durable and must not hold queue or session state as the only copy.

rules.rule: IF write rate or working-set size exceeds the largest single instance AND caching, read replicas and archiving are already exhausted THEN shard. IF any cheaper option remains untried THEN do NOT shard.
rules.plain: Splitting a database across many machines is the last resort. Try caching, read copies and deleting old data first. Sharding is a one-way door.
rules.why: Sharding removes cross-shard transactions, cross-shard joins, global unique constraints and easy schema migrations, and makes re-sharding a multi-month project. The largest RDS and Aurora instances carry very large workloads; most we-need-to-shard conclusions are a missing index or an unbounded table.
rules.trigger: db.write_iops_p99 > 0.7*max_single_instance_capacity AND caching_exhausted=true AND archiving_exhausted=true
rules.exception: If the data model is natively partitioned by tenant from day one and tenant isolation is required anyway, shard by tenant EARLY - it is cheap to design in and brutal to retrofit. DynamoDB and Aurora Limitless shard for you.

rules.rule: Encryption at rest MUST be decided AT CREATION for RDS, Aurora and EBS - it cannot be enabled in place and requires a snapshot, encrypted copy and restore, with downtime. Turn on EBS account-level default encryption in EVERY Region. For services encrypted by default (DynamoDB always, S3 with SSE-S3 since Jan 2023, SQS with SQS-owned keys since 2023) the meaningful question is the KEY TYPE, not on or off.
rules.plain: Encrypt databases and disks when you create them, not later. For DynamoDB, S3 and SQS the data is already encrypted - the real decision is whose key.
rules.why: Retrofitting encryption on a live RDS instance is a migration project, so enabling the EBS account default converts this from a per-resource discipline into a property of the account. Checking encryption_at_rest=false against DynamoDB can NEVER fire, because DynamoDB encryption cannot be disabled - a check written that way is a check that does nothing.
rules.trigger: (resource_type IN (EBS,RDS,Aurora,EFS,Redshift) AND encryption_at_rest=false) OR (resource_type IN (DynamoDB,S3,SQS,SNS) AND key_type=aws_owned AND data_classification=sensitive) OR (region.ebs_default_encryption=false)
rules.exception: EBS default encryption blocks sharing unencrypted AMIs and snapshots publicly and prevents launching from some community AMIs - copy them encrypted first. Keep the honest caveat: encryption at rest defends against disk and snapshot theft and mis-shared snapshots; it does NOT defend against a compromised application credential, which is what most breaches actually use.

rules.rule: Delete or alarm on: unattached EBS volumes; PUBLIC IPv4 ADDRESSES you do not need (every one is billed hourly whether attached or not); load balancers with zero requests; RDS instances with zero connections AND zero read/write IOPS over 30 days; idle SageMaker real-time endpoints; provisioned concurrency under-utilised; idle NAT gateways; unused interface endpoints; orphaned snapshots.
rules.plain: These keep charging you while doing nothing: spare disks, spare IP addresses, empty load balancers, databases nobody connects to and reserved capacity nobody calls.
rules.why: Every one bills on provisioned time, not use. The public IPv4 picture changed on 1 Feb 2024: AWS now charges about $0.005/hour for EVERY public IPv4 address, associated or not - including addresses on running instances, load balancers, NAT gateways and public RDS endpoints - so the finding is no longer an unassociated Elastic IP but a high public IPv4 COUNT, and at fleet scale that is a material, invisible line item. An idle GPU-class SageMaker endpoint can exceed $1,000/month serving zero requests, and a stopped EC2 instance still bills its EBS volumes.
rules.trigger: (ebs.state=available) OR (public_ipv4_count > required_public_ipv4_count) OR (elb.request_count_7d=0) OR (rds.connections_30d=0 AND rds.io_30d=0) OR (sagemaker_endpoint.invocations_7d=0) OR (lambda.provisioned_concurrency_utilization<0.2)
rules.exception: Deliberately warm DR standbys, provisioned concurrency pre-warmed for a known launch, and addresses held to preserve a partner allow-list entry are legitimate - tag them so the sweeper skips them. Beware two false positives: read replicas and month-end-only databases will show zero connections, and a STOPPED RDS instance is automatically restarted by AWS after 7 days and resumes full billing, so a naive weekend schedule silently fails.

rules.rule: Set a retention policy on EVERY log group - the default is never expire - and enforce it at creation, because retention is per log group and is NOT inherited. Then address the larger half: INGESTION (about $0.50/GB in us-east-1) usually dwarfs storage (about $0.03/GB-month), so move high-volume, low-query groups to the Infrequent Access log class.
rules.plain: CloudWatch log groups keep logs forever by default and you pay storage forever. Set an expiry on every one - and remember you pay far more to put logs in than to keep them.
rules.why: Debug logging switched on during an incident and never switched off produces a line item that grows for years, and a retention-only fix addresses the smaller half of the bill. The usual sources are VPC Flow Logs and verbose Lambda or container logging. Retention must also match the incident-review window: 7-day retention means the evidence is gone before the postmortem.
rules.trigger: service=CloudWatchLogs AND (log_group.retentionInDays IS NULL OR retention_days < incident_review_window_days OR (monthly_ingest_gb>100 AND log_class!=INFREQUENT_ACCESS AND query_frequency=low))
rules.exception: Audit, security and regulatory logs with a legal retention period belong in S3 (via subscription filter or Firehose) with a lifecycle policy, not in CloudWatch Logs at CloudWatch prices. The Infrequent Access log class does not support Live Tail, metric filters or subscription filters, so check what you lose before switching.

rules.rule: Cover the provably stable baseline with a commitment and leave the rest On-Demand or Spot. Compute Savings Plans cover EC2, Fargate AND Lambda across any family and Region and survive a re-platform; EC2 Instance Savings Plans are family- and Region-locked at a deeper discount; Standard RIs are deepest but locked to a family. Savings Plans and RIs are NOT cancellable and NOT refundable for the whole term. In an Organization, commitments are SHARED across accounts by default, so a single account buying its own is usually wrong.
rules.plain: Commit for one or three years to the amount of compute you never drop below, not your average or your peak. Buy it once for the whole organisation, not per account.
rules.why: A commitment above your baseline is billed whether or not you use it, and a three-year all-upfront on a workload you migrate off in year one is a total loss. Standard RIs are locked to a family, so a move to Graviton or Fargate strands them - Savings Plans convert an architecture decision into a reversible one. Consolidated billing also aggregates volume-tiered pricing, which is a separate argument for one payer and many accounts.
rules.trigger: steady_state_hours_per_month>500 AND commitment_coverage_ratio < baseline_ratio AND org_level_sharing_evaluated=false
rules.exception: Commitment SIZING is a risk-appetite decision, not a technical fact: committing only to the 90-day trough is one defensible policy and is conservative enough to leave savings on the table for a stable fleet; Cost Explorer's recommendation engine optimises on a different basis. Standard RIs can be resold on the Marketplace (Linux, shared tenancy) but that needs seller registration, a US bank account and 30 days remaining - it is not a liquid exit; Savings Plans cannot be sold or cancelled at all. Convertible RIs can be exchanged. Capacity Reservations, not Savings Plans, buy capacity guarantees. Headline discount percentages are maxima.

rules.rule: IF environment is dev, test or staging AND non-serverless resources run 168 hours a week THEN attach a start/stop schedule. A weekday 8-hour schedule removes about 76% of the HOURS (40 of 168) - it does NOT remove 76% of the SPEND. Compute the actual saving per account before quoting a number.
rules.plain: Turn off development and test servers at night and at weekends. You use them about forty hours a week out of a hundred and sixty-eight - but the bill does not fall by the same proportion.
rules.why: Stopping an EC2 instance does not stop EBS volume charges, public IPv4 charges, or any Savings Plan or Reserved Instance commitment already bought - if non-prod sits under a Compute Savings Plan, a schedule can save almost nothing unless production absorbs the freed commitment. For RDS, a stopped instance still bills storage and backups AND is automatically restarted by AWS after 7 days, so a naive weekend schedule silently fails.
rules.trigger: environment!=production AND resource_type IN (EC2,RDS) AND uptime_hours_per_week>60 AND scheduler_attached=false
rules.exception: Shared staging used across time zones, long-running test fixtures, and anything holding expensive-to-rebuild state. Serverless and Fargate Spot already bill on consumption and need no schedule. Aurora Serverless v2 with min_capacity=0 achieves the same outcome without a scheduler.

rules.rule: Activate cost allocation tags in the payer account and enforce owner, environment and service tags AT CREATION with Organizations tag policies plus an SCP conditioned on aws:RequestTag - a Config rule only detects after the fact. Measure the tagged ratio over TAGGABLE spend only.
rules.plain: Tag everything with who owns it and what it is for, and block creation without the tags. If you cannot say who owns a cost, nobody will ever reduce it.
rules.why: Cost Explorer and the CUR can only group by dimensions that exist, so untagged spend is one undifferentiated blob and every conversation becomes opinion. Correcting a common claim: tagging IS partially retroactive - Cost Explorer supports cost allocation tag BACKFILL (StartCostAllocationTagBackfill, one request per 24 hours, up to 12 months), which applies a tag's active status to prior months for resources that ALREADY CARRIED the tag. What is genuinely unrecoverable is history for a resource that was untagged at the time of usage.
rules.trigger: activity=cost_optimization AND (cost_allocation_tags_activated=false OR tagged_share_of_taggable_spend<target_ratio OR tag_enforcement_at_creation=false)
rules.exception: Some charges cannot be tagged at all - inter-service data transfer, support, tax, some Marketplace fees - and can be 5-15% of a bill, so a 95% target measured over TOTAL spend is unreachable and the rule will always fire. Attribute untaggable spend by ACCOUNT boundary instead, which is itself an argument for one account per team and environment.

rules.rule: Every account needs an AWS Budget with actual AND forecast alerts plus a Cost Anomaly Detection monitor - but these are DETECTIVE and lag up to about 24 hours. Against the runaway-spend threat (a leaked key mining crypto, a recursive Lambda) they MUST be paired with PREVENTIVE controls: SCPs denying expensive Regions, families and services; service quotas lowered to intended maxima; GuardDuty for credential-compromise findings; and Budget actions.
rules.plain: Set a spending alarm and turn on automatic anomaly alerts before you deploy anything - then add the controls that actually stop the spend, because the alerts arrive a day late.
rules.why: AWS bills in arrears with no hard stop. Cost and Usage Report data refreshes up to about 24 hours behind and anomaly detection typically alerts within about 24 hours of the spike; against an unbounded GPU fleet that is already a catastrophic bill. Correcting a common claim: Cost Anomaly Detection is free, but AWS Budgets is free only for the FIRST TWO budgets per account and then costs about $0.02 per budget per day, with Budget actions charged separately - an org stamping six budgets into 200 accounts is paying real money for governance.
rules.trigger: account.budgets_count=0 OR account.anomaly_monitors=0 OR preventive_spend_controls=false
rules.exception: In an Organization, monitors and budgets can be centralised in the management account with per-linked-account scope rather than duplicated everywhere; the requirement is coverage, not one object per account.

rules.rule: Right-size on PERCENTILES over at least 14 days, never on averages, and consolidate genuinely idle hosts. Use p99 of 1-minute DETAILED monitoring (not 5-minute aggregates, which hide a 20-second spike) plus max, and FIRST assert that the metric exists - memory is not collected by default and needs the CloudWatch agent or Application Signals, so missing must not be read as low.
rules.plain: If a server never gets busy even at its peak over two weeks, make it smaller. Judge by its busiest moments, not its average - and check you are actually collecting the numbers before concluding anything.
rules.why: Average hides the peak the capacity exists for: a box at 8% average and 95% p99 is correctly sized. Consolidation is also a sustainability and cost finding in one - two hosts at 30% utilisation are less efficient than one at 60% because of per-host baseline draw, and you pay full price for an idle instance either way. Compute Optimizer applies this analysis and is free over a 14-day lookback; the 93-day lookback is the paid enhanced tier.
rules.trigger: service IN (EC2,RDS,ECS,Lambda) AND observation_days>=14 AND metrics_present=true AND cpu_p99<0.4 AND mem_p99<0.4
rules.exception: Headroom reserved deliberately for spikes, N+1 failover capacity, and workloads bound by memory, I/O or licence rather than CPU - measure the actual binding resource first. Per-core licensed (Oracle, SQL Server), burstable T-family, instance-store-backed, GPU and latency-critical workloads break this rule. Downsizing also often halves the instance's EBS and network bandwidth allowance, which can be the real constraint - make that a hard check, not a caveat.

rules.rule: IF reducing cost or latency on reads THEN add caching from the outside in and stop at the first layer that solves it: client and browser Cache-Control, then CDN/CloudFront, then application in-memory or ElastiCache, then a database result cache or read replica. Never add a database replica to solve a problem a Cache-Control header solves.
rules.plain: Cache as close to the user as you can. A cached response in the browser or CDN never touches your servers. Adding database copies is the most expensive answer.
rules.why: Each layer inward costs more per request and adds a component that can fail. CloudFront also has cheaper per-GB egress than direct EC2 egress and does not charge for origin fetches from AWS origins, so CDN caching cuts request load and transfer cost simultaneously.
rules.trigger: proposed_fix IN (read_replica,bigger_db) AND response_is_cacheable=true AND (cdn_exists=false OR cache_hit_ratio<0.8)
rules.exception: Personalised, authenticated or rapidly-changing responses cannot be cached at the edge in full - cache the shared fragments and static assets and let only the personalised sliver go inward. The ordering inverts for write-heavy paths. Two preconditions the rule depends on: you must be able to state a STALENESS BUDGET per endpoint, and Cache-Control on an authenticated response is how private data leaks into a shared cache. Any claim that cost rises by a fixed multiple per layer is invented.

rules.rule: IF a team self-manages a component AWS offers as a managed service (self-hosted Kafka, self-patched MySQL on EC2, a homemade cron scheduler) AND no documented capability gap exists THEN record the reason or migrate.
rules.plain: If AWS already runs it for you and you are running it yourself for no stated reason, you are paying staff to do a job you could rent.
rules.why: Self-managed infrastructure cost is dominated by engineer hours and 3am pages, which never appear on the AWS bill and so never surface in a cost review.
rules.trigger: self_managed_component IN managed_service_catalog AND justification IS NULL
rules.exception: Real capability gaps exist: specific Kafka versions or plugins, database extensions RDS does not allow, licensing and residency constraints, and cases where the managed per-unit price exceeds total self-managed cost at very large steady scale. The rule demands the reason be written down, not that migration always happens.

rules.rule: IF sustainability goals are claimed THEN require a PER-UNIT-OF-WORK KPI (kgCO2e or kWh per transaction, per user) and model growth to reduce impact intensity. Absolute totals alone are not a KPI.
rules.plain: Measure emissions per customer or per transaction, not just the total. Total always rises when the business grows, which tells you nothing.
rules.why: The pillar requires comparing productive output with total impact per unit of work, and architecting so growth reduces intensity. Absolute totals conflate business growth with inefficiency, so they cannot identify regressions - which is the stated purpose of having the goals.
rules.trigger: sustainability_goal_exists=true AND kpi_denominator IS NULL
rules.exception: Workloads with flat, non-growing demand can track absolute consumption meaningfully. The AWS Customer Carbon Footprint Tool reports at account granularity and lags by months, so per-transaction figures are usually MODELLED from usage, not measured - say so rather than implying measurement.

rules.rule: IF a mutating (readOnly=false) CloudTrail event in a production account was made with CONSOLE session credentials by a principal that is not a declared break-glass role THEN raise a violation, open an incident ticket and require the change be reproduced in code within one working day.
rules.plain: In production, nobody clicks buttons in the console to change things. Changes come from code. If someone does it by hand, an alarm fires and they must put it into code the next day.
rules.why: A console change exists only in one person's head: the next IaC deploy silently reverts it, or the resource becomes un-reproducible in DR. Every long outage postmortem contains the sentence this setting had been changed manually and nobody knew.
rules.trigger: account.env=production AND cloudtrail.readOnly=false AND cloudtrail.userIdentity.sessionContext.attributes.sessionCredentialFromConsole=true AND principal NOT IN break_glass_roles
rules.exception: A declared incident under an audited break-glass role, where the change is logged and back-ported to code before the incident closes. Some resources genuinely have no IaC coverage (Marketplace subscriptions, the account support plan) and must be allow-listed explicitly. Two detection corrections that matter: CloudFormation-driven changes do NOT carry eventSource=cloudformation.amazonaws.com (the record carries the underlying service's eventSource with cloudformation.amazonaws.com as the userAgent), so excluding on eventSource flags every CFN change as console; and console userAgent strings are unreliable, appearing variously as a browser string, AWS Internal, or signin.amazonaws.com. Use sessionCredentialFromConsole plus readOnly, not a userAgent or eventName regex.

rules.rule: IF two workloads differ in environment (prod versus non-prod), data classification or compliance scope THEN they MUST live in separate AWS accounts under one Organization, not in separate VPCs or under separate IAM roles of one account. The management account runs NO workloads; add dedicated security and log-archive accounts.
rules.plain: Dev and prod must be different AWS accounts. Not different tags, not different roles - different accounts. It is the only wall that cannot be accidentally opened by a bad IAM policy.
rules.why: An IAM policy is a filter that must be right every time, written by many people over years; an account is a default-deny wall enforced by AWS, and it also gives per-environment service quotas, blast-radius-limited credential compromise and clean cost attribution. Most we-deleted-prod-by-mistake events are a correct command in the wrong terminal.
rules.trigger: organization.account_count=1 AND (env_count>1 OR contains_regulated_data=true) OR workloads_in_management_account=true
rules.exception: A genuinely single-tenant hobby or spike workload with no customer data and no revenue - and even then, prod in its own account is the minimum. Account count is not the constraint: the default maximum is 10 accounts per organization, increases are granted up to 50,000, but NEW organizations may start BELOW 10, so request the increase before the design review. Separation alone does not stop a cross-account role doing the same damage - pair it with an SCP denying prod-role assumption from non-prod principals. Account sprawl without centralised logging, an org trail and Identity Center creates many blind spots.

rules.rule: SCPs have NO effect on principals in the MANAGEMENT ACCOUNT and cannot restrict service-linked roles - this cannot be configured away, and resource control policies (RCPs) share the same management-account carve-out. Plan around the attachment and size quotas: 5 policies of each type per root, OU or account, and 5,120 bytes per policy document; inherited policies do not count against the per-target limit, so push shared denies UP the OU tree.
rules.plain: Service control policies do not apply to the management account or to service-linked roles, and they never grant anything - they only take away. You can attach only five to any one target, so keep them tidy.
rules.why: Teams that put production in the management account believe they are guarded when they are not. And these quotas are discovered mid-incident, when one more deny is needed. Effective permission is the INTERSECTION of SCP and RCP and identity policy and resource policy and permissions boundary and session policy and VPC endpoint policy - every one must allow, and an explicit deny anywhere wins.
rules.trigger: (workload_account=management_account) OR (scps_attached_to_target>=4) OR (scp_document_bytes>4000)
rules.exception: Keep the management account empty except for Organizations, billing and the org trail; delegate administration to a member account, noting that delegated admins are ordinary member accounts and ARE subject to SCPs. Console-saved policies have whitespace stripped before counting, so a policy that fits via the console may fail via the CLI or SDK where the document is stored byte for byte - size checks must assume the CLI behaviour.

rules.rule: Attach a root- or OU-level SCP denying at minimum: disabling CloudTrail, GuardDuty, Config, Security Hub, Inspector or Macie; deleting flow logs, KMS keys or S3 Object Lock configuration; downgrading ec2:ModifyInstanceMetadataOptions; leaving the organization; changing account contacts; and acting outside approved Regions (aws:RequestedRegion). Pair it with an RCP denying access to YOUR RESOURCES from principals outside aws:PrincipalOrgID, which an SCP cannot do.
rules.plain: Put a short deny-list at the top that stops anyone turning off logging, leaving the org, or building in unapproved regions - and a resource-control policy that stops outsiders reaching your data at all.
rules.why: These are the first moves of both an attacker with admin and a well-meaning engineer in a hurry, and a deny in an SCP cannot be overridden by any identity policy in a member account including its root user - the only control with that property. SCPs constrain YOUR PRINCIPALS; RCPs (generally available since Nov 2024) constrain ACCESS TO YOUR RESOURCES. A governance baseline without RCPs is a 2023 baseline.
rules.trigger: organizations.all_features=true AND (scp_denies_logging_tamper=false OR rcp_org_perimeter=false)
rules.exception: Exempt the security and audit role ARNs or they cannot do their job - but aws:PrincipalArn exemptions are bypassable if anyone can create a role with that name or path, so pin them with a path you control via a permissions boundary. Global services (IAM, STS, CloudFront, Route 53, Organizations, Support) must be excluded from an aws:RequestedRegion deny using NotAction or you break the account. Never attach a new SCP to the org root untested - pilot on one OU.

rules.rule: AWS Organizations caps OU nesting at FIVE levels below a root, with one root per organization. Design for that from day one. The 2,000-OU figure is a default quota and can be raised; the nesting depth cannot.
rules.plain: Your account folder structure can only be five folders deep. Design for that at the start.
rules.why: Org structures are migrated painfully: moving accounts changes inherited SCPs, which can instantly break running workloads. Hitting the depth limit two years in forces a re-parenting exercise across live production accounts.
rules.trigger: planned_ou_depth>5
rules.exception: None for the depth. Do not present the OU COUNT as immovable - it is a default maximum and increases can be requested.

rules.rule: IF the team has no owner for remote state and locking THEN prefer CloudFormation or CDK (AWS-managed state, no state file to corrupt). IF the estate spans non-AWS providers or you need a true plan-before-apply diff across providers THEN prefer Terraform or OpenTofu AND fund the state backend (versioned S3 plus locking, per environment) as a first-class production system.
rules.plain: Pick CloudFormation or CDK if you are AWS-only and small - AWS keeps the state for you. Pick Terraform if you manage things outside AWS too, but then the state file is itself production and needs backups and locking.
rules.why: The honest trade-off is state ownership and blast radius, not syntax. CloudFormation rolls back automatically but its failure modes (UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED, stuck stacks, resource-already-exists) need import surgery. Terraform gives a real plan and multi-provider reach, but a lost or unlocked state means orphaned or double-created resources, and a destroy on the wrong workspace is the modern console-in-prod. CDK is CloudFormation underneath: you inherit its limits and add a synth step whose output must be diffed, not trusted.
rules.trigger: iac_tool_selection AND (state_backend_owner IS NULL OR multi_provider_required)
rules.exception: Existing team skill dominates: a Terraform-fluent AWS-only team should stay on Terraform, because tool churn costs more than the theoretical win. CloudFormation-only features (StackSets across an Organization) and regulatory demands for AWS-native tooling push the other way.

rules.rule: Do not treat CloudFormation drift detection as coverage. It skips unsupported resource types (NOT_CHECKED), properties left at defaults, KMSKeyId, Lambda function Code and secret-valued properties, and a parent-stack detect does NOT descend into nested stacks. Treat NOT_CHECKED as UNVERIFIED, run detection per nested stack, and separately detect resources that belong to NO stack at all by diffing a Config or Resource Explorer inventory against stack resources.
rules.plain: CloudFormation can tell you if someone changed things by hand, but only for supported resources and only for properties you explicitly wrote. No drift found often just means it did not look - and it never sees resources created outside any stack.
rules.why: Teams read IN_SYNC as proof of integrity when it is proof of nothing for those resources. The larger gap is unmanaged resources: drift cannot flag something that was never in a stack, and that is where most manual estate lives.
rules.trigger: drift_check_enabled=true AND (nested_stacks_checked=false OR not_checked_treated_as_compliant=true OR unmanaged_resource_inventory_diff=false)
rules.exception: DetectStackDrift is throttled and slow on large estates - use the Config managed rule cloudformation-stack-drift-detection-check or an organization conformance pack rather than a polling loop. Drift can also report false positives where service-supplied array defaults or equal-but-differently-expressed units (1024 MB versus 1 GB) appear as NOT_EQUAL.

rules.rule: IF a stateful resource (RDS or Aurora, DynamoDB, EFS, S3, EBS) is defined in a CloudFormation or CDK stack THEN set BOTH DeletionPolicy AND UpdateReplacePolicy to Retain or Snapshot, enable stack TERMINATION PROTECTION, and add resource-level deletion protection (RDS deletion protection, DynamoDB deletion protection, S3 Object Lock or MFA-free bucket policies). Back it with an SCP denying DeleteDBCluster, DeleteBucket and ScheduleKeyDeletion outside break-glass.
rules.plain: Mark your databases so that deleting or updating the stack cannot delete them - and turn on the resource's own deletion protection too.
rules.why: UpdateReplacePolicy is INDEPENDENT of DeletionPolicy and a property change that forces replacement (renaming a DB identifier, changing an immutable property) destroys the data during a routine update with no stack delete involved. CDK's removalPolicy sets both. This is the most common self-inflicted permanent data loss in IaC.
rules.trigger: resource.type IN stateful_types AND (DeletionPolicy IN (null,Delete) OR UpdateReplacePolicy IN (null,Delete) OR stack.termination_protection=false OR resource.deletion_protection=false)
rules.exception: Three corrections to the usual framing. CloudFormation DEFAULTS DeletionPolicy to Snapshot for several types (AWS::RDS::DBInstance without a read replica, AWS::RDS::DBCluster, AWS::ElastiCache::CacheCluster, AWS::Redshift::Cluster, AWS::Neptune::DBCluster), so the default is not always Delete. Retain has its own trap: a retained resource blocks re-creating the stack with the same physical name and leaves orphaned, unmanaged, still-billing resources, so pair it with a documented reconciliation step. And a STACK POLICY only guards updates made through CloudFormation - it does not apply to a stack delete; termination protection is the control for that. DynamoDB, S3 and EFS have no Snapshot policy, only Retain. Ephemeral preview environments with disposable data are exempt if tagged as such.

rules.rule: IF a deployment writes to N targets THEN the pipeline MUST verify the deployed artifact DIGEST on all N targets before declaring success, and MUST halt and alarm when confirmed_count < N. Never report success on partial fleet coverage.
rules.plain: If you deploy to eight servers, check that all eight actually got the new code. Knight Capital deployed to seven of eight and lost about 440 million dollars in roughly 45 minutes.
rules.why: Knight Capital's 1 Aug 2012 loss was a deploy that reached seven of eight production servers, leaving the eighth running legacy code whose repurposed flag re-activated dead logic. The lesson is that partial deployment produces a state nobody has ever tested: N-1 new plus 1 old. Any tool that reports success on a subset (CodeDeployDefault.AllAtOnce succeeds if even one instance succeeds) hides exactly this.
rules.trigger: deploy_targets_total != deploy_targets_confirmed_at_expected_digest
rules.exception: A deliberate canary or linear rollout, where the partial state is intended, time-boxed, designed to be safe with mixed versions, and monitored. The rule forbids UNINTENDED partial state, not staged rollout.

rules.rule: IF a config flag, feature-flag key, API field or message field is being reused for NEW semantics THEN reject the change: require a new name, and require the old code path to be deleted in a separate, EARLIER release.
rules.plain: Never recycle an old switch for a new purpose. Give the new thing a new name, and delete the old code first, in its own release.
