rules.why: Knight's flag was reused while the code it used to control still existed on at least one host. Reuse converts old code is dormant into old code is armed. The safe sequence is: stop referencing the old path, ship and verify the deletion, only then reuse the name - and preferably never reuse it.
rules.trigger: config_key_semantics_changed=true AND old_code_path_removed=false
rules.exception: If an external contract forces the key name, version the VALUE schema instead and keep the old branch explicitly implemented rather than dead.

rules.rule: IF a schema change is destructive (DROP COLUMN, RENAME, adding NOT NULL, narrowing a type) THEN split it into three separately deployed releases - expand (add nullable or new, dual-write), migrate and verify (backfill, read from new, old still present), contract (remove old) - and never ship expand or contract in the same deploy as the code that depends on it.
rules.plain: Never rename or delete a database column in the same release as the code change. Add the new column, write to both, move reads over, and only much later delete the old one.
rules.why: During any rolling, canary or blue/green deploy, old and new application code run simultaneously against ONE database. A destructive migration makes the old code invalid the instant it runs, so rollback becomes impossible precisely when you need it. Expand and contract is what makes rollback a real option instead of a slide in the runbook.
rules.trigger: migration_type IN (drop_column,rename_column,add_not_null,narrow_type) AND deployed_in_same_release_as_dependent_code=true
rules.exception: A table with a single writer that is provably offline (batch-only, maintenance window, or a brand-new table nothing reads yet). Very large backfills need throttling and a resumable job rather than one migration step. Note also that RDS storage cannot be SHRUNK - a genuine one-way door in the same class.

rules.rule: IF a change is irreversible - data deleted or overwritten in place, an outbound side effect already emitted (email, payment, webhook), a consumed schema field removed, a key rotated and the old one destroyed - THEN a rollback plan is not acceptable. Require a TESTED roll-forward path, a pre-change backup with a PROVEN restore, and an explicit named approver.
rules.plain: Some things cannot be undone: money sent, emails delivered, data deleted, keys destroyed. For those, we will roll back is a lie.
rules.why: Rollback restores code, not consequences. Teams write rollback: redeploy previous version on changes where the previous version cannot read the migrated data or where the side effect already left the building. Naming the irreversible class in advance is what forces the extra safeguards to be funded.
rules.trigger: change_class IN (destructive_data,emitted_side_effect,removed_consumed_field,key_destroyed) AND rollback_listed_as_mitigation=true
rules.exception: If the side effect is idempotent and replayable end to end (event-sourced with an authoritative log, or a payment provider with reliable idempotency keys) rollback can be genuine - but it must be DEMONSTRATED, not asserted.

rules.rule: Choose the deployment strategy from reversibility, statistical power and cost. Canary when the change is schema-compatible AND the bake window will contain ENOUGH EVENTS to detect the target regression rate. Linear or blue/green with a full synthetic test before cutover when traffic is too low or bursty for a slice to carry signal. Blue/green when duplicate capacity is affordable and instant rollback is required. IF the change touches shared persistent state THEN no traffic-shifting strategy is sufficient without expand and contract first.
rules.plain: Canary when you have enough traffic to see a problem in the first slice. Blue/green when you can afford two full environments and need to switch back instantly. None of these help if the database change itself is unsafe.
rules.why: Strategy choice is a statistics problem: a 10% canary on 50 requests a minute tells you nothing before the bake window ends. The right condition is required SAMPLE SIZE at your chosen power, not a fixed requests-per-second threshold - a 50 rps service with a 1% error SLO can canary fine over a longer bake. Blue/green buys instant rollback at 2x capacity plus a session and connection-draining problem.
rules.trigger: deploy_strategy_selection USING (schema_compatible, events_in_bake_window, duplicate_capacity_affordable, touches_shared_state)
rules.exception: With a NETWORK Load Balancer, CodeDeploy for ECS supports ONLY CodeDeployDefault.ECSAllAtOnce - no canary or linear. Blue/green no longer implies CodeDeploy: ECS supports native blue/green under the ECS deployment controller with lifecycle hooks. CloudFormation-managed ECS blue/green is unavailable in some Regions. Also decide whether errors are user-visible immediately or only in a nightly batch, because that sets the bake window.

rules.rule: IF canary_bake_minutes <= (alarm_evaluation_periods * alarm_period_minutes) + metric_publication_lag THEN the canary CANNOT fail. Require bake_time >= 2x detection time, or shorten the alarm.
rules.plain: If your canary shifts all traffic after five minutes but your alarm needs fifteen minutes of data to fire, the canary is theatre.
rules.why: CodeDeploy canary configurations promote on a TIMER, not on evidence. With a 5-minute CloudWatch alarm at 3 evaluation periods you need about 15 minutes plus publication lag before the alarm can breach, while Canary10Percent5Minutes promotes at 5. Countless the-canary-passed incidents are this arithmetic error.
rules.trigger: bake_minutes < 2*(alarm_periods*period_minutes + publication_lag_minutes)
rules.exception: Where rollback is driven by a high-resolution sub-minute metric, or by a synthetic canary that exercises the path deterministically inside the window, a short bake is defensible because detection is genuinely fast.

rules.rule: IF an ECS service uses the rolling (ECS) deployment controller THEN enable deploymentCircuitBreaker with rollback=true. Understand the threshold: with BOUNDED_PERCENT it is clamp(ceil(value/100 * desiredCount), 3, 200) where value defaults to 50 - so the minimum of 3 bites whenever ceil(value/100*desiredCount) < 3, which at the default is any desiredCount below 6 but at value=25 is any below 12. For faster rollback use thresholdConfiguration type=COUNT with an explicit small value and resetOnHealthyTask=false; for very large fleets use UNBOUNDED_PERCENT, which removes both bounds.
rules.plain: Turn on ECS automatic rollback, and compute the actual failure threshold rather than assuming - for small services it will always tolerate at least three failed tasks before giving up.
rules.why: With resetOnHealthyTask=true (the default) only CONSECUTIVE failures count, so a flapping task can loop far longer than operators expect. And if there is no prior deployment in COMPLETED state, the circuit breaker cannot roll back at all and the deployment simply stalls.
rules.trigger: deployment_controller=ECS AND (circuit_breaker_enabled=false OR ceil(threshold_value/100*desired_count)<3)
rules.exception: The circuit breaker is supported ONLY for the rolling (ECS) deployment controller; services using CODE_DEPLOY or EXTERNAL controllers use CodeDeploy alarms and hooks instead. A hardcoded desiredCount<6 check is wrong in general - compute it from the configured percentage.

rules.rule: IF a task definition, Lambda image, Helm chart or launch template references a container image WITHOUT an @sha256 digest THEN reject it. Record the deployed digest in the deployment record, and protect the digest: ECR lifecycle policies and pull-through caches can DELETE an image a live task definition still pins, so exclude referenced digests from expiry rules.
rules.plain: Never deploy latest. Deploy the exact image fingerprint, write it down in the deploy log, and make sure nothing can delete that image later.
rules.why: A mutable tag means the artifact you tested and the artifact that runs can differ, and a scale-out event hours later can pull a different image than the original deploy - a mixed fleet nobody deployed. Digest pinning also makes the Knight-style are-all-N-at-the-same-digest check mechanically possible and makes rollback exact rather than approximate.
rules.trigger: image_reference NOT MATCHES @sha256: OR (ecr_lifecycle_policy_exists AND NOT excludes_digests_referenced_by_live_task_definitions)
rules.exception: Base images in a Dockerfile during development, and pipelines that resolve a tag to a digest at BUILD time and pin the digest downstream - the rule is about what reaches runtime, not what a human types. Do not test on the presence of a colon: a registry-with-port reference and a digest reference both contain one. ECR tag mutability is no longer two-valued - it has MUTABLE, IMMUTABLE, IMMUTABLE_WITH_EXCLUSION and MUTABLE_WITH_EXCLUSION with tag-prefix filters, so a check accepting only IMMUTABLE false-positives on the exclusion modes most teams adopt. Digest pinning proves sameness, not provenance: add signing and a trusted-builder attestation for that.

rules.rule: The load balancer health check must be a SHALLOW liveness check that proves this target can serve requests, with a SEPARATE deep health signal used only for alarms and dashboards. Then do the arithmetic: time_to_remove = HealthCheckIntervalSeconds * UnhealthyThresholdCount + HealthCheckTimeoutSeconds. At the instance and IP defaults (interval 30, unhealthy threshold 2, timeout 5) a broken target keeps receiving traffic for roughly 65 seconds.
rules.plain: The load balancer should check that this one box works, not whether the database is up - otherwise one database hiccup takes every server out at once. And by default a dead server keeps getting traffic for about a minute.
rules.why: Two opposite failure modes. A too-shallow check (a static 200 from the web server) keeps routing to processes whose thread pool is exhausted. A too-deep check couples every instance's health to a SHARED dependency and converts a degraded dependency into a total outage. On timing, teams assume removal is instant; it is interval times threshold. Recovery is deliberately slower than failure - a returning target needs HealthyThresholdCount (default 5) consecutive successes.
rules.trigger: health_check_exercises_downstream_dependency=true OR health_check_returns_static_response=true OR (interval_seconds*unhealthy_threshold + timeout_seconds) > error_budget_seconds_per_event
rules.exception: Interval is tunable 5-300 seconds and thresholds 2-10, so interval 5 with threshold 2 cuts removal to about 15 seconds at the cost of more health-check load on an already struggling target. Lambda targets have different defaults (timeout 30, interval 35). Set deregistration_delay below p99 request duration only if requests are idempotent. The ALB mitigates the worst case by FAILING OPEN - if all targets in all enabled AZs are unhealthy it routes to them anyway - but never design on fail-open. A thin adapter whose only function is to reach one dependency may justifiably include it, with capacity isolation.

rules.rule: The scaling metric MUST change in proportion to capacity: use ALBRequestCountPerTarget or a custom per-instance metric such as backlog-per-instance, not raw CPU on an I/O-bound, queue-driven or connection-bound workload, and enable 1-minute detailed monitoring plus group metrics. Then set default_instance_warmup to at least the MEASURED p95 time-to-first-healthy-request, and use a warm pool when that time is large.
rules.plain: Scale on requests per server or backlog per worker, not CPU, unless CPU is really what runs out. And tell Auto Scaling how long a new server takes to be useful, or it will keep launching more.
rules.why: AWS explicitly lists metrics that do NOT work for target tracking: total ELB RequestCount, Latency, and SQS ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible, because backlog does not divide by fleet size - the documented remedy is a custom backlog-per-instance metric. On warmup: until it expires an instance is excluded from the group's aggregated metrics, so if warmup is too short the cold instance is counted, its bad metrics drag the average, and the policy launches more - the classic cold-start amplification loop.
rules.trigger: (scaling_policy.metric=ASGAverageCPUUtilization AND workload_bottleneck!=cpu) OR (measured_p95_ready_seconds > configured_instance_warmup_seconds) OR detailed_monitoring=false
rules.exception: Genuinely CPU-bound workloads (transcoding, compression, CPU inference) should use CPU target tracking. Do not repeat the claim that target tracking cannot scale in - it scales BOTH ways; the real requirement is a valid utilisation metric that varies inversely with capacity. AWS recommends default instance warmup for ALL groups as the replacement for cooldown with target tracking. Warm pools cost EBS storage for stopped instances and full instance hours in Running state; hibernation has instance-family and volume-encryption prerequisites. Any minutes threshold for using a warm pool is a rule of thumb.

rules.rule: IF a job is scheduled (EventBridge Scheduler, cron, Step Functions timer) THEN it MUST write a last_successful_run timestamp to durable storage on success, AND a separate CloudWatch alarm MUST fire when now - last_successful_run > expected_interval * 2, with treatMissingData set to BREACHING. Alarming only on the job's error metric is insufficient.
rules.plain: A scheduled job must prove it ran, not just complain when it fails. If it never starts at all, an error alarm stays quiet forever.
rules.why: The dangerous scheduled-job failure is silence: the rule got disabled, the target's permission was revoked, the account hit a quota, or the invocation never happened - and error-based alarms have no signal in that case. A positive heartbeat converts absence into an alarmable condition. Without treatMissingData=breaching a missing metric leaves the alarm in INSUFFICIENT_DATA forever and it never fires.
rules.trigger: scheduled_job_exists AND (heartbeat_record_written=false OR staleness_alarm_exists=false OR alarm.treat_missing_data!=breaching)
rules.exception: Jobs whose absence is self-evident within minutes through a downstream business metric that is ALREADY alarmed and TESTED - assumed is not enough. All date logic in the heartbeat must use one declared timezone.

rules.rule: A production workload MUST have at least one alarm bound to a USER-VISIBLE symptom or business KPI (orders per minute, successful logins, checkout error rate, SLO burn rate), not only infrastructure metrics. And routing follows the same line: cause-based alarms (CPU high, disk 80%, pod restarted, queue non-empty) go to a ticket or dashboard; only symptoms that are provably user-affecting page a human.
rules.plain: Alerts on CPU do not tell you the checkout is broken. Alert on what customers feel, and only wake someone for that.
rules.why: CPU-only monitoring misses the entire class of failures where the servers are healthy and doing the wrong thing: a bad deploy returning 200 with an empty cart, a dependency returning stale data, a payment provider rejecting everything. Cause-based paging produces alert fatigue, and alert fatigue is a causal factor in long outages - the real page arrives among twenty false ones and is acknowledged without being read. Symptom alarms also survive architecture change.
rules.trigger: environment=production AND (count(alarms WHERE metric_class=business_or_sli)=0 OR EXISTS alarm WHERE routes_to_pager=true AND metric_class=cause AND user_impact_proven=false)
rules.exception: A pure infrastructure platform with no business transaction of its own legitimately alarms on technical SLIs - but then those SLIs ARE its KPIs and must be defined as such. Cause alarms that are imminent and irreversible page legitimately: disk filling on a stateful node with a known short time-to-full, certificate expiry inside 72 hours, a hard service quota within 10% of being hit. These are you-have-hours-not-minutes alarms and they are few.

rules.rule: IF the error budget consumed this period exceeds 100% THEN freeze feature releases for that service and route the team to reliability work until it recovers. IF the SLO target is 100%, or five nines with no stated business reason, THEN reject the SLO as unengineered. State whether the window is rolling or calendar.
rules.plain: Decide how much downtime is acceptable, measure it, and when you have used it all, stop shipping features and fix reliability. Never set the target at 100%.
rules.why: An error budget is the software equivalent of a structural safety factor: it makes acceptable failure explicit and turns ship-fast-versus-be-reliable from an argument into arithmetic. Users on a 99% mobile connection cannot perceive the difference between 99.99% and 99.999% backend availability, so the extra nine is spend with no return. A rolling 28-day window behaves very differently from a calendar quarter, so the policy must say which it uses.
rules.trigger: budget_consumed_pct>100 AND feature_release_requested=true
rules.exception: A fix that reduces burn, a security patch, and a genuinely regulatory-deadline change - each with a named approver.

rules.rule: IF a request crosses a service boundary (ALB to service to SQS to Lambda to database) THEN a correlation or trace id MUST be generated at the edge, propagated in headers AND message attributes, emitted in every structured log line, and preserved across ASYNCHRONOUS hops. IF any hop drops it THEN treat that hop as unobservable.
rules.plain: Give every incoming request an id at the front door and carry it through every service, queue and log line.
rules.why: Monitoring answers is it broken; observability answers why, for this specific request. Without an id that survives the asynchronous hops, a distributed failure can only be reconstructed by timestamp guessing. Queues are where propagation most often breaks, because the id must be moved from an HTTP header into a message attribute by hand.
rules.trigger: service_boundary_crossed AND correlation_id_present_in_downstream_logs=false
rules.exception: Fire-and-forget telemetry paths with no debugging value. X-Ray sampling means a trace may not exist for every request, so the LOG correlation id must be independent of whether the request was sampled. Budget the cost: high-cardinality CloudWatch custom metrics and PutMetricData charges can exceed the compute they observe - prefer EMF to emit metrics from logs and cap metric cardinality explicitly.

rules.rule: IF an alarm pages a human THEN its description or SNS payload MUST link a runbook stating the user-visible symptom, the first diagnostic query, the safe mitigation and the escalation path; any step not executed within the staleness window is marked UNVERIFIED. IF an on-call shift ends THEN a WRITTEN handover MUST record open incidents, change freezes, in-flight deployments and canaries not yet fully promoted, silenced alarms WITH their expiry, and error budget consumed.
rules.plain: Every alarm that wakes someone must link to a page telling them what it means and what to do first. And when you hand over on-call, write down what is still broken, what is half-deployed, and which alarms you turned off and when they come back.
rules.why: At 03:00 the on-call engineer's working memory IS the runbook; without one every incident starts with a 20-minute rediscovery phase. Runbooks rot faster than code because nothing compiles them. The most dangerous operational state is a half-finished change owned by someone who has gone home - a canary at 10%, an alarm silenced for an hour six hours ago - and suppressed alarms without a recorded expiry are how known-issue mitigations become permanent blind spots.
rules.trigger: (alarm.routes_to_pager=true AND (runbook_url IS NULL OR runbook.last_verified_days>staleness_window_days)) OR (shift_end_event AND (handover_document_written=false OR suppressed_alarms_without_expiry>0))
rules.exception: Alarms whose mitigation is fully automated still need a link - it documents what the automation DID, not what the human should type. A single-person rotation still needs the record, because it is the input to the postmortem and to the person's own memory a week later. The 90-day staleness mark is a convention, not a derived figure.

rules.rule: Ship small, reversible changes and PROVE the rollback before the change ships. Measure batch size with proxies a pipeline actually has - merged PRs or commits per release, files or lines changed, number of services touched in one deploy, time since the previous deploy - not with an unmeasurable notion of one logical change.
rules.plain: Ship small changes you can undo. Big batched releases make it impossible to tell which change broke things.
rules.why: Blast radius scales with batch size and mean-time-to-identify scales with the number of changes in flight: a release containing thirty changes forces a full rollback of twenty-nine good ones, or a risky forward fix under pressure. The load-bearing half of this rule is the TESTED rollback, because a condition like changes_per_deploy>1 fires on essentially every deploy and gets the rule switched off.
rules.trigger: rollback_tested=false OR services_touched_per_deploy>1 OR days_since_previous_deploy>batch_window_days
rules.exception: Coupled schema-and-code migrations that genuinely cannot be split must ship together - but then expand and contract, not a single cutover, is the correct shape, and rollback is tested against the expanded schema.

rules.rule: IF an IaC template pins an Availability Zone by literal NAME or by a fixed INDEX into the AZ list THEN it is a hidden single-AZ dependency: replace it with a dynamic lookup across at least two AZs, and use AZ IDs (for example use1-az1) where physical correlation genuinely matters.
rules.plain: Never write a zone name or a fixed zone position into a template. Ask for the zones instead.
rules.why: Hardcoded AZs silently pin subnets, ASGs and databases to one zone, so the multi-AZ diagram on the wall is not what is deployed. AWS also randomises AZ-name-to-physical-AZ mapping per account, so the same literal means different physical zones in different accounts - which is why AZ IDs exist.
rules.trigger: iac_template pins az_by_literal_name=true OR iac_template pins az_by_fixed_index=true
rules.exception: Deliberate zonal pinning for a latency-, licence- or co-location-bound workload must be pinned by AZ ID with a written reason. Some resources legitimately require a specific AZ in the template (an EBS volume co-located with its instance, single-AZ file systems, Outposts, Local Zone, Wavelength and Dedicated Host placement). Be aware this is NOT reliably detectable by a simple regex: a naive pattern misses multi-token Regions, Local and Wavelength zones, and cannot see a fixed list index at all - detecting the index form needs an AST or plan-level check.

rules.rule: Root cannot be restricted by ANY IAM policy - only an Organizations SCP constrains it, and only in member accounts. Therefore: root MUST have no access keys; root MUST have MFA (hardware key or passkey) where it still has credentials; and for MEMBER accounts the correct 2026 posture is to REMOVE root credentials entirely using Organizations centralized root access management. Alarm on CloudTrail events where userIdentity.type=Root.
rules.plain: The root login must never have API keys. Turn on MFA where root still exists - and in member accounts, delete the root credentials altogether using central root access management.
rules.why: A leaked root key is total, irreversible account compromise: the holder can delete every resource, every backup and every trail, and change the account email. AWS now enforces root MFA on management accounts. But a correctly hardened member account may have NO root password or MFA at all because the credentials were removed - a naive enable-root-MFA check would FAIL that account, which is backwards.
rules.trigger: (principal=root AND access_key_count>0) OR (account_type=standalone_or_management AND root_mfa_enabled=false) OR (account_type=member AND root_credentials_management_enabled=false AND root_credentials_removed=false)
rules.exception: There is NO exception permitting root access keys - and specifically, the claim that AWS GovCloud (US) lacks root console sign-in and therefore needs root keys is FALSE and must not be used to justify them. Root legitimately fires for a small documented set of tasks (closing the account, changing the support plan, some S3 and CloudFront actions), so tune the alarm to page a human rather than deleting it, and store the MFA device where two people can reach it. SMS MFA has not been supported for IAM since 2019, so never-use-SMS is dead advice.

rules.rule: IF an IAM user has a console login profile (the machine-checkable signal of a human) THEN replace it with IAM Identity Center or federated role assumption issuing temporary credentials.
rules.plain: People should log in through single sign-on and assume roles, not have their own permanent AWS usernames and keys.
rules.why: IAM users carry long-lived credentials that outlive the employee, the laptop and the incident. Federation gives credentials with a lifetime measured in hours, centrally revocable by disabling the identity in the IdP - one off-boarding action instead of one per account. This is AWS's first-listed IAM best practice.
rules.trigger: resource_type=iam_user AND login_profile_exists=true AND break_glass=false
rules.exception: Break-glass users (see the break-glass rule). Genuinely forced IAM-user cases are now rare and the usual list is stale: AWS CodeCommit has been closed to new customers since 25 July 2024 so its Git credentials are not a live reason, and Amazon Keyspaces supports SigV4 with IAM roles as well as service-specific credentials. What survives is legacy service-specific credentials and SFTP/Transfer-style service users. Re-date this list before relying on it.

rules.rule: IF a workload runs on EC2, ECS, EKS or Lambda AND obtains credentials from a static access key THEN FAIL: attach an IAM role (instance profile, task role, IRSA or EKS Pod Identity, execution role).
rules.plain: Code running on AWS should get its permissions from an attached role, not from keys pasted into config.
rules.why: Every AWS compute service delivers rotating temporary credentials automatically. A static key in an environment variable, AMI, container image or dotenv file is a permanent secret that will eventually be committed, logged or exfiltrated - and unlike a role, it does not expire.
rules.trigger: compute_service IN (EC2,ECS,EKS,Lambda) AND (env CONTAINS AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY OR credentials_file_present=true)
rules.exception: Workloads genuinely outside AWS - and even then prefer IAM Roles Anywhere (X.509), AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity (for example GitHub Actions OIDC), or SSM hybrid activations before a long-lived key. On ECS, keep the TASK role and the task EXECUTION role distinct: conflating them routinely gives application code permission to read every secret in the account.

rules.rule: An IAM user may hold a MAXIMUM OF 2 access keys, so a create-migrate-verify-delete rotation is IMPOSSIBLE for a user that already has two - delete the unused one first. Flag keys older than the rotation interval or unused for that long; delete keys never used and older than the creation grace period, but only after a CloudTrail lookback confirms it.
rules.plain: Old keys and keys nobody has used should be removed - but you can only hold two keys per user, so clear the spare before you rotate.
rules.why: Every surviving key is a permanent liability with no compensating benefit if unused. The credential report plus access-key-last-used makes this machine-checkable, but last-used is not fully reliable: it has reporting lag and has not historically covered every service and Region, so a key can show never used and still be live. Do not auto-delete on last-used alone.
rules.trigger: resource_type=access_key AND (age_days>rotation_interval_days OR last_used_days>rotation_interval_days OR (last_used=never AND age_days>grace_days)) AND cloudtrail_lookback_confirms_unused=true
rules.exception: A key wired into a third-party SaaS integration may need a coordinated change window - schedule it, do not exempt it. Blind time-based rotation on a key you cannot test can itself cause the outage. The 90-day interval is a convention.

rules.rule: IF a repository or artifact scan matches (AKIA|ASIA)[0-9A-Z]{16} THEN treat it as an ACTIVE INCIDENT in this order: attach the AWSCompromisedKeyQuarantineV3 managed policy to the principal, deactivate or revoke, then rotate, then review CloudTrail and enumerate created resources in EVERY Region including opt-in ones. Run secret scanning both pre-commit AND server-side.
rules.plain: An AWS key in a repo is already leaked. Quarantine the principal first, then kill the key, then find out what it did - in every region.
rules.why: Public-repo crawlers find exposed keys in seconds to minutes and the usual payload is bulk GPU and EC2 mining across every Region. Deleting the commit does not help - git history, every fork and every clone still have it. Pre-commit hooks are optional on the developer's machine, so server-side scanning is the only enforceable half.
rules.trigger: scm_or_artifact_scan.match=true AND (quarantine_applied=false OR deactivated=false)
rules.exception: Documentation examples using the literal AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE are not findings. CRITICALLY, ASIA (temporary STS) credentials are NOT lower urgency: a session token is valid for up to 12 hours (role chaining 1 hour, GetSessionToken up to 36 hours) and rotating the role's trust policy does NOT revoke an already-issued session. The documented revocation is a deny policy on the role conditioned on aws:TokenIssueTime - the AWSRevokeOlderSessions inline policy the console generates - or deleting the role.

rules.rule: IF an EC2 instance's metadata options have HttpTokens != required THEN FAIL. Set HttpTokens=required per instance, set the account and Region defaults with ModifyInstanceMetadataDefaults (read with GetInstanceMetadataDefaults), and enforce org-wide with an Organizations declarative policy for EC2. Set HttpPutResponseHopLimit from the NETWORKING MODE, not from a vague container flag.
rules.plain: Force EC2 instance metadata to require a session token, set the account-wide default, and limit how far metadata replies can travel.
rules.why: IMDSv1 answers an unauthenticated GET to 169.254.169.254, so any SSRF, open proxy or vulnerable app on the box can read the instance role's credentials - the exact mechanism of the 2019 Capital One breach. IMDSv2 requires a PUT to obtain a token, which a reflected or SSRF request cannot normally perform, and the hop limit stops the response escaping the host.
rules.trigger: service=EC2 AND metadata_options.HttpTokens!=required
rules.exception: Hop limit is genuinely networking-mode dependent and getting it wrong breaks credential retrieval: ECS on EC2 with awsvpc or host networking works at 1, while Docker default bridge and ECS bridge mode need 2; EKS with IRSA or Pod Identity should use 1 PLUS a pod-egress block to 169.254.169.254. Enumerate IMDSv1 callers with the MetadataNoToken CloudWatch metric before flipping. Note there is no field called HttpTokensEnforced - use the API names above or the rule is not checkable. Also check that the condition tests for != required rather than = optional, so instances with absent or pending metadata options do not silently pass.

rules.rule: IF a principal is granted IAM write permissions THEN condition the grant on iam:PermissionsBoundary matching an approved boundary AND on a role path or name prefix. Cover the FULL escalation set, not three actions: CreateRole, PutRolePolicy, AttachRolePolicy, UpdateRole, CreateUser, CreateAccessKey, CreatePolicyVersion, SetDefaultPolicyVersion, UpdateAssumeRolePolicy, and iam:PassRole to a privileged role via ec2:RunInstances, lambda:CreateFunction, glue or cloudformation. The boundary must deny BOTH iam:DeleteRolePermissionsBoundary AND iam:PutRolePermissionsBoundary.
rules.plain: If developers can create IAM roles, force every role they create to carry a ceiling policy - and close every other way of escalating, including passing a privileged role to a new instance or function.
rules.why: CreateRole plus AttachRolePolicy is effectively AdministratorAccess: create a role with star-on-star, assume it, and the original restriction is gone. But a boundary conditioned on only those actions does NOT make the grant safe - CreatePolicyVersion rewrites an attached policy in place, UpdateAssumeRolePolicy takes over an existing privileged role, and swapping in a weaker boundary is as good as deleting it.
rules.trigger: identity_policy allows any_of(iam_write_actions) AND (condition iam:PermissionsBoundary absent OR boundary_denies_put_and_delete_boundary=false OR passrole_unscoped=true)
rules.exception: Central platform and security admins who are supposed to hold real IAM power - small, named, MFA-gated and monitored. A boundary is a ceiling, not a grant: it never gives permission on its own and never replaces the identity policy. Permissions boundaries do NOT constrain resource-based policies or service-linked roles.

rules.rule: Detect EFFECTIVE admin, not the literal string star. A statement with Action=* and Resource=* is the easy case; Action lists of service-wide wildcards, NotAction with a thin exclusion, and a meaningless Condition that is always true all grant admin while passing a string check. Use IAM Access Analyzer policy validation and policy generation plus unused-access findings, and the policy simulator, to judge.
rules.plain: No hand-written policy should effectively allow everything. Checking for a literal asterisk is not enough - people get around it without meaning to.
rules.why: Least privilege is only checkable if you write it as a constraint and then verify the constraint. Access Analyzer generates a policy from up to 90 days of CloudTrail activity for a role and runs over 100 validation checks including this-grants-more-than-you-probably-meant, and unused-access findings tell you which granted actions were never used.
rules.trigger: iam_policy.effective_admin=true AND policy NOT IN (named_break_glass_roles)
rules.exception: A deliberate break-glass AdministratorAccess role, and short-lived sandbox accounts with no real data. Be honest about the start-broad-then-tighten pattern: it is how most over-permissive policies become permanent, so if you allow it, it MUST carry a machine-checkable expiry (a date tag enforced by a separate rule) or it is not a rule, it is permission.

rules.rule: A cross-account request is allowed only if BOTH the identity policy in the calling account AND the resource policy (or role trust policy) in the owning account allow it - AWS runs two independent evaluations and an explicit Deny anywhere wins. A resource policy alone is sufficient ONLY within the same account.
rules.plain: Cross-account access needs a yes from both accounts. Inside one account, a resource policy alone can be enough.
rules.why: Engineers lose hours because same-account behaviour differs: there, a bucket policy naming the account principal can suffice. Knowing which evaluation is failing tells you which account to fix - and getting it wrong sends people to fix the wrong account, which is the failure this rule exists to prevent.
rules.trigger: request.principal_account != resource.account AND (identity_policy_allow=false OR resource_policy_allow=false)
rules.exception: Role trust policies are NOT an exception to this: a cross-account sts:AssumeRole still needs the trust policy in the trusting account to allow the principal AND an identity policy in the calling account allowing sts:AssumeRole on that role ARN. The genuine same-account special case is that within one account a resource policy can grant access without a matching identity policy for most services. SCPs, RCPs, session policies, VPC endpoint policies and RAM permission fragments can each veto on top.

rules.rule: IF a role trust policy names a principal OUTSIDE your organization (a vendor or SaaS account) THEN it MUST require sts:ExternalId with a value YOU generated, and MUST NOT use Principal star or a bare account root without conditions.
rules.plain: When you give a vendor a role, require a secret ExternalId they must send. Never trust their whole account without it.
rules.why: Without an ExternalId you are exposed to the confused-deputy problem: the vendor's other customers share that vendor's account, and any of them who learn your role ARN can ask the vendor to assume it. The ExternalId must be unpredictable and issued by YOU, not chosen by the vendor.
rules.trigger: iam_role.trust_policy.principal.account NOT IN organization_accounts AND condition sts:ExternalId absent
rules.exception: For trust between accounts inside your own Organization use aws:PrincipalOrgID instead. AWS service principals (for example lambda.amazonaws.com) use aws:SourceArn and aws:SourceAccount for the same purpose.

rules.rule: Enable all four S3 Block Public Access settings at the ACCOUNT level (s3:PutAccountPublicAccessBlock is the action to protect with an SCP, not the bucket-level one), and set Object Ownership to BucketOwnerEnforced so ACLs are ignored and all access is expressed in the bucket policy. S3 applies the most restrictive of organization, account and bucket settings.
rules.plain: Turn off public S3 access for the whole account, not bucket by bucket, and turn ACLs off so there is only one place to get access wrong.
rules.why: Per-bucket settings fail because there is always a new bucket created by a script or a vendor tool; the account-level setting covers buckets that do not exist yet. ACLs are a pre-IAM access system evaluated in parallel with policies, and AuthenticatedUsers notoriously means any AWS customer on earth. Buckets created since April 2023 default to BPA on and ACLs disabled, so legacy accounts and legacy buckets are where the exposure still lives.
rules.trigger: account.public_access_block.all_true=false OR bucket.public_access_block.all_true=false OR bucket.object_ownership IN (ObjectWriter,BucketOwnerPreferred)
rules.exception: A genuine public static website or public dataset belongs in its OWN account with no other data, served through CloudFront with OAC while the bucket stays private, and documented. Turning BPA off again INSTANTLY re-exposes any pre-existing public policy or ACL - BPA masks, it does not delete. Do not over-claim: BPA is not the only control that covers future buckets (SCPs and Control Tower guardrails also do), and it does NOT close the modern exposure paths - a permissive bucket POLICY, presigned URLs, cross-account access points, an over-broad VPC endpoint policy, or a public CloudFront distribution over a private bucket. Denying s3:PutBucketPolicy wholesale breaks replication, OAC and legitimate cross-account access, so scope the deny by condition and pair it with IAM Access Analyzer external-access findings. Legacy cross-account writers that set canned ACLs will get AccessControlListNotSupported - migrate the writer; CloudFront, ELB and CloudTrail log delivery all support the ACL-free model.

rules.rule: IF an RDS or cluster snapshot attribute restore contains all THEN it is world-readable - FAIL immediately. Enable the per-account, per-Region EBS Snapshot Block Public Access and AMI Block Public Access settings, and apply the same check to Redshift, DocumentDB and Neptune snapshots, ECR repositories, Lambda function resource policies with Principal star, SNS and SQS policies, and OpenSearch domains. Alarm on ModifyDBSnapshotAttribute and ModifyDBClusterSnapshotAttribute with ValuesToAdd=all.
rules.plain: Never mark a snapshot or machine image public. Anyone with an AWS account can restore it and read your whole database, and it leaves no access log.
rules.why: A public snapshot is a full copy of the database handed to the internet - worse than a public S3 object because it is the entire schema and every row. It is one CLI flag away and is repeatedly found by researchers scanning public snapshot listings. Detect it with describe-db-snapshot-attributes, not by eye.
rules.trigger: snapshot.attribute.restore CONTAINS all OR ami.public=true OR ebs_snapshot.public=true OR account.ebs_snapshot_block_public_access=false OR lambda.resource_policy.principal=* OR ecr.repository_public=true
rules.exception: Genuinely public sample datasets only, in an isolated account. Two useful facts: ENCRYPTED snapshots CANNOT be shared publicly at all, which is one more argument for encrypting every database; and private sharing is capped at 20 AWS accounts per manual snapshot.

rules.rule: IF a bucket, queue, topic or table has a resource policy THEN it MUST include a Deny on aws:SecureTransport=false with a minimum TLS version condition. IF an ALB, NLB or API listener accepts port 80 THEN it MUST only redirect to 443.
rules.plain: Refuse unencrypted connections in the resource policy itself, and make plain HTTP only redirect to HTTPS.
rules.why: Server-side enforcement is the only kind that counts: a client can always choose http or a bad SDK configuration. The aws:SecureTransport deny makes the service itself reject the request, so it holds for every caller including ones you do not control.
rules.trigger: resource_policy lacks Deny on aws:SecureTransport=false OR (listener.protocol=HTTP AND action!=redirect)
rules.exception: Very old clients that cannot do TLS 1.2 - fix the client. A port-80 listener is legitimate solely as a 301 to HTTPS and for ACME HTTP-01 challenges. Note aws:SecureTransport in an S3 bucket policy also blocks unencrypted access from inside a VPC through a gateway endpoint, which is intended.

rules.rule: IF an application needs a credential THEN it MUST fetch it at runtime from Secrets Manager or SSM Parameter Store SecureString using the workload's IAM role. Plaintext secrets in environment variables, task definitions, IaC templates or AMIs FAIL. Rotation must be CONFIGURED and PROVEN to have run - check LastRotatedDate, not just that rotation is enabled.
rules.plain: Keep passwords in Secrets Manager or SSM and fetch them when the app runs. Do not paste them into config, templates or images. And check that rotation actually ran.
rules.why: Environment variables leak into logs, crash dumps, process listings, Lambda console views and CloudFormation stack outputs - all readable by principals with far weaker permissions than the secret deserves. A managed store gives per-secret IAM, KMS encryption, CloudTrail access records and rotation, and centralises revocation. An unrotated secret sitting in Secrets Manager is still an unrotated secret.
rules.trigger: (lambda.environment OR ecs.task_definition.environment OR iac_template) CONTAINS literal_credential_value OR (secret.rotation_enabled=true AND days_since_last_rotated>rotation_interval_days)
rules.exception: Secrets Manager costs about $0.40 per secret per month plus API calls; Parameter Store SecureString is free in the standard tier and is fine where you do not need automatic rotation or cross-Region replication. Cache for the container lifetime and handle rotation by retrying once on auth failure - fetching on every invocation costs money and latency. The strongest form is to have no database password at all: use RDS IAM database authentication.

rules.rule: An Organization MUST have at LEAST one organization CloudTrail: multi-Region, log file validation ON, delivering to an S3 bucket in a SEPARATE log-archive account whose bucket policy workload accounts cannot alter, with S3 Object Lock in compliance mode on the log bucket, its own data-event coverage, a retention period matched to the incident-review window, and restricted read access.
rules.plain: One org-wide CloudTrail, all regions, writing to a locked bucket in a different account that nobody can delete from - and only the security team can read it.
rules.why: CloudTrail is the only account-level record of who did what, and an attacker's second move after gaining admin is to stop the trail or empty the bucket. A separate account with Object Lock means compromising the workload account does not destroy the evidence. Log file validation gives a signed digest so you can prove nothing was altered, and multi-Region catches activity in Regions you do not use - precisely where attackers go. Read access to logs is itself sensitive.
rules.trigger: cloudtrail.is_organization_trail=false OR is_multi_region_trail=false OR log_file_validation_enabled=false OR log_bucket.account=workload_account OR log_bucket.object_lock=false
rules.exception: Do NOT require exactly one trail - organizations commonly run an org management-event trail plus scoped data-event trails. Do NOT pair MFA Delete with Object Lock: MFA Delete can only be enabled by the ROOT USER of the bucket-owning account using root credentials, which contradicts the root-credentials rule, and Object Lock already prevents version deletion and is the AWS-recommended control here. Data events are charged per event and can dominate the bill on high-volume buckets - scope them to sensitive prefixes. Management events are free for the first trail only, and an org trail plus a local member-account trail is the common accidental double charge. An org trail does not cover accounts that LEAVE the org. Consider CloudTrail Lake as the retention and query layer.

rules.rule: GuardDuty is the RUNTIME threat detector (is something bad happening now) and must be enabled in EVERY Region from a delegated administrator with auto-enable for new accounts. Security Hub CSPM is the POSTURE aggregator (is something misconfigured) and MOST of its controls are AWS Config rules - with the Config recorder off they never evaluate and the console still looks green. Enabling one does not cover the other, and neither works without Config recording on, org-wide, in every Region.
rules.plain: GuardDuty spots attacks in progress; Security Hub CSPM scores your settings. You need both, and both need AWS Config switched on or the checks silently never run.
rules.why: GuardDuty reads duplicated streams of CloudTrail management events, VPC Flow Logs and Route 53 Resolver DNS queries directly - you do not have to enable those logs and it does not change your configuration. It catches the real breach patterns: credentials used from a new ASN, crypto-mining DNS, disabled logging, S3 anomalies. Regions you never use are exactly where mining instances get launched. Conversely GuardDuty will never tell you a bucket is public.
rules.trigger: guardduty.regions_enabled<all_regions OR guardduty.delegated_admin=false OR guardduty.auto_enable_new_accounts=false OR (securityhub.enabled=true AND config.recorder_enabled=false)
rules.exception: Naming has changed: the posture and controls product is now AWS Security Hub CSPM, while AWS Security Hub refers to the newer unified risk-prioritisation product - a rule written against the old naming will confuse anyone reading the current console. Not ALL controls are Config-backed; some use direct API calls, so the correct statement is most, not all. GuardDuty cannot see DNS queries if you use a non-AWS resolver, so that detection channel silently goes dark. Config is billed per configuration item and per rule evaluation and can become a top-five line item in churn-heavy accounts - scope recorded resource types or use periodic recording rather than switching it off, and know exactly which controls you blinded.

rules.rule: IF a VPC carries production or regulated traffic THEN enable VPC Flow Logs at the VPC LEVEL for ALL traffic, to S3 or CloudWatch Logs with a defined retention, INDEPENDENTLY of GuardDuty, and include the newer fields (pkt-srcaddr, pkt-dstaddr, flow-direction, traffic-path).
rules.plain: Turn on VPC Flow Logs for production, even though GuardDuty already reads flow data.
rules.why: GuardDuty consumes its own duplicate flow stream and then discards it - it gives you findings, not records. During an incident you need the raw flows to answer what else did that host talk to and how much left. Enabling at the VPC level covers new subnets and ENIs automatically, and without the newer fields NAT and load-balanced traffic is unattributable.
rules.trigger: vpc.environment=production AND flow_logs_enabled=false
rules.exception: Flow logs to CloudWatch Logs cost roughly an order of magnitude more than to S3 at ingest and storage - on chatty VPCs send to S3 in Parquet with a lifecycle policy and query with Athena. Flow logs do NOT capture packet contents, DNS to the Amazon resolver, instance-metadata traffic to 169.254.169.254, or Windows licence activation traffic, so do not treat them as complete. Pair with Reachability Analyzer and Network Access Analyzer to verify intended paths rather than only recording actual ones.

rules.rule: IF an account is in an Organization THEN an IAM Access Analyzer external-access analyzer MUST exist with the ORGANIZATION zone of trust, and every finding MUST be resolved or explicitly archived with a documented reason. Run the unused-access analyzer alongside it.
rules.plain: Run Access Analyzer with the whole organization as the trusted zone, and clear every someone-outside-can-reach-this finding.
rules.why: Access Analyzer uses automated reasoning over the actual policies rather than pattern matching, so it PROVES whether an external principal can reach a resource - catching combinations a human misses, such as a bucket policy plus a KMS key policy plus a role trust. Setting the zone of trust to the organization makes internal sharing silent so only genuinely external access alerts.
rules.trigger: organization.member_account=true AND access_analyzer.type=ORGANIZATION NOT EXISTS
rules.exception: Deliberate external sharing (a partner bucket, a vendor role) should be archived with an archive rule and a written justification so the queue stays at zero and a new finding is genuinely new. Access Analyzer covers a FIXED LIST of resource types, so absence of findings is not proof of no external access.

rules.rule: IF the only path to the console or API is a federated identity provider THEN an IdP outage locks you out during the incident. Maintain a small number of break-glass IAM roles assumable only by a break-glass principal with HARDWARE MFA that is NOT issued by the same IdP, credentials split under dual control in an offline safe, a login test on a schedule, and CloudTrail plus EventBridge alerting on every use.
rules.plain: Keep a few emergency logins that do not depend on your single sign-on working - and test them regularly, or they are as good as absent.
rules.why: Identity is the dependency nobody models: a federated-only estate means an identity failure removes your ability even to diagnose. The MFA device and the credential vault must not themselves federate through the IdP, or you have rebuilt the circular dependency. Alerting on every use is what stops the break-glass path becoming the attack path.
rules.trigger: federated_only=true OR break_glass_principals=0 OR days_since_break_glass_login_test>test_interval_days OR break_glass_mfa_issued_by_primary_idp=true
rules.exception: Do NOT justify this with the claim that IAM Identity Center is tied to us-east-1 - it is deployed in a customer-chosen home Region. What IS us-east-1 backed is IAM WRITES; IAM authorization and regional STS are not. The one genuine exception above this rule is the Organizations management account root, which is the ultimate break-glass and is governed by centralized root access management and root sessions rather than by this rule. Long-lived access keys on a break-glass user are themselves a regression many orgs cannot accept - prefer an assumable role.

rules.rule: AWS owns hardware, the AWS global infrastructure and the virtualization layer. The CUSTOMER always owns: guest OS and application patching on IaaS (EC2, ECS on EC2, self-managed EKS nodes); and, for EVERY service however managed, data classification, encryption choices, IAM permissions and network configuration. For SHARED controls (patch management, configuration management, awareness training) the customer half must have a NAMED OWNER and evidence - assert it against the Customer Responsibility or complementary user entity controls matrix in the AWS Artifact SOC and ISO reports.
rules.plain: AWS patches the physical machine; you patch the operating system inside your instance. And no matter which service you use, who can access your data and whether it is encrypted is always your job. Some controls are split in half - your half does not happen unless someone is assigned to it.
rules.why: Beginners assume cloud means managed and run unpatched kernels for years, and the compromise is contractually and operationally theirs. Every large public S3 breach has been a customer-side permission mistake on infrastructure AWS was operating correctly - it is a managed service is never a defence for an open bucket or a wildcard policy. Auditors and engineers read shared as covered, but AWS compliance reports cover only AWS's half.
rules.trigger: (compute_type=ec2 AND patch_automation_configured=false) OR (resource_policy grants broad external access) OR (encryption_key_choice_undocumented=true) OR (control IN shared_controls AND customer_side_owner IS NULL)
rules.exception: Managed node groups, Fargate, Bottlerocket, EKS Auto Mode and immutable AMI pipelines shift the MECHANICS and, for EKS Auto Mode and Fargate, genuinely put node OS lifecycle on AWS - but you still own the container image contents and the version you choose. Only fully abstracted services (Lambda, S3, DynamoDB) remove OS patching from your side. Any staleness threshold used to operationalise the patching half (for example an AMI age in days) is a heuristic of yours, not a documented fact, and must not inherit this rule's certainty. Be precise about the AWS side: on Nitro much of the historical hypervisor is offloaded to hardware, so AWS's own wording is hardware, global infrastructure and the virtualization layer.

rules.rule: Enable Amazon Inspector for EC2, ECR and Lambda across the organization from a delegated administrator, and track Systems Manager Patch Manager compliance. Unpatched software is how the credential everything else protects gets stolen in the first place.
rules.plain: Scan your instances, container images and functions for known vulnerabilities, and track patch compliance. Otherwise all the identity controls guard a box someone has already broken into.
rules.why: The shared-responsibility rule assigns guest OS and application patching to you, but assignment without a scanner and a compliance number is not a control. Inspector continuously scans rather than running on a schedule, which matters because a vulnerability disclosed today affects images built last year.
rules.trigger: inspector_enabled=false OR patch_compliance_reporting=false OR critical_findings_older_than_sla>0
rules.exception: Fully abstracted services remove the OS from scope, but Lambda function DEPENDENCIES and container image contents remain yours. Scope Inspector deliberately: ECR continuous scanning of a large registry has a real cost, and lifecycle-expiring unused images is usually the right first step.

rules.rule: Protect the domain layer: registrar transfer lock and registrar account MFA, DNSSEC where supported, and a scheduled sweep for DANGLING DNS records pointing at released AWS resources (an S3 bucket, CloudFront distribution, Elastic IP or ELB name you no longer own).
rules.plain: Lock your domain, turn on MFA at the registrar, and delete DNS records that point at AWS resources you have deleted - otherwise someone else can claim them.
rules.why: Subdomain takeover through a dangling CNAME is cheap, common and entirely preventable: an attacker re-creates the released resource name and serves content from your domain, inheriting cookies, trust and sometimes certificate issuance. It is also invisible to every control in this rule base because nothing is misconfigured inside your account - the record simply points at nothing you own.
rules.trigger: dns_record.target_resource_exists=false OR registrar.transfer_lock=false OR registrar.mfa=false
rules.exception: Records deliberately pointing at third-party SaaS endpoints are legitimate but must be inventoried, because the same takeover applies when the SaaS subscription lapses.

rules.rule: IF an application is internet-facing THEN put AWS WAF on the CloudFront distribution, ALB or API Gateway stage, AND prevent ORIGIN BYPASS: the ALB must not accept traffic that did not come through CloudFront (restrict by the CloudFront managed prefix list plus a shared secret header, or use VPC origins), and S3 origins must be private behind OAC.
rules.plain: Put a web firewall in front of anything on the internet, and make sure nobody can skip it by hitting the load balancer directly.
rules.why: A WAF on CloudFront is useless if the ALB's DNS name is publicly resolvable and accepts direct traffic - attackers find the origin and bypass every edge rule, including rate limiting and bot control. This is the most common gap between an architecture diagram that shows a WAF and a system that has one.
rules.trigger: internet_facing=true AND (waf_attached=false OR origin_accepts_direct_traffic=true OR (s3_origin AND oac_absent))
rules.exception: Shield Advanced adds DDoS response team access and cost protection and is justified by the value at risk, not by default. WAF managed rule groups are charged per rule group plus per request, so choose them deliberately rather than enabling everything.

rules.rule: Before an incident: set the account ALTERNATE SECURITY CONTACT in every account (AWS abuse notices go there and are routinely missed), maintain a monitored security-account role into every member account, write and TEST an IR runbook, and confirm the security team can reach logs and quarantine a principal without the workload team's help.
rules.plain: Make sure AWS can reach you, the security team can get into every account, and somebody has actually rehearsed the response.
rules.why: AWS sends abuse and compromise notifications to the account contacts; when those are a departed employee's mailbox the first signal of a compromise is the bill. And an IR plan that requires the workload team to grant access at 3am is not a plan - the whole point is that the workload account may be the compromised one.
rules.trigger: account.alternate_security_contact IS NULL OR security_account_role_present=false OR days_since_ir_exercise>exercise_interval_days
rules.exception: None worth taking for a production account. The security role must itself be monitored and alarmed on use, or it becomes the attack path - the same condition that applies to break-glass.

rules.rule: IF an incident is declared THEN a blameless postmortem MUST produce corrective actions with a named OWNER and a due date, and a separate check MUST confirm the action actually shipped (a commit, a merged PR, a deployed change) rather than that it was written down.
rules.plain: After an incident, write down what will change, who owns it and when - then verify it actually shipped. Untracked actions are why the same incident happens again.
rules.why: Every other rule here is discovered the expensive way through an incident; without tracked corrective actions the learning evaporates and the same outage recurs. Status backed by a commit, not by memory, is the only honest register - this is the natural complement to the on-call handover rule.
rules.trigger: incident_closed=true AND (corrective_actions_count=0 OR EXISTS action WHERE owner IS NULL OR due_date IS NULL OR shipped_evidence IS NULL)
rules.exception: An incident with a genuinely external, uncontrollable cause may close with a detection or degradation improvement rather than a fix - but that is still a tracked corrective action with an owner.

decisionTrees.question: Which compute primitive should this workload run on?

branches.if: A single unit of work can exceed 900 seconds, or its input size is unbounded
branches.then: Not Lambda. Use Step Functions to decompose, AWS Batch for a deep queue of independent jobs, or ECS/Fargate for a long-running process
branches.because: The Lambda function timeout of 900 seconds is a hard, non-increasable quota; only Lambda Managed Instances async and event-source-mapping invocations reach 5,400 seconds

branches.if: Work is event-driven and idle most of the time, and each unit fits inside the timeout and the 6 MB sync payload
branches.then: Lambda, sized by AWS Lambda Power Tuning rather than by observed memory, with reserved concurrency where it shares a pool with critical functions
branches.because: Lambda bills GB-ms with no idle charge, and CPU scales with the memory setting so the cheapest setting is measured, not guessed

branches.if: The workload is a long-running service with steady traffic and you cannot name an owner for node patching and scaling
branches.then: Fargate, or ECS Managed Instances if you want EC2 rates without owning the hosts
branches.because: Fargate removes host operations at a per-task premium; ECS Managed Instances gives EC2-rate compute with AWS-managed patching and scaling, which removes the old reason to pay the Fargate premium

branches.if: You can keep EC2 hosts genuinely full and have a team to run them, or you need GPUs, privileged mode, placement constraints or Docker volume drivers
branches.then: ECS or EKS on EC2, with Graviton where arm64 is viable and Spot for the interruptible share on a price-capacity-optimized, diversified mixed-instances policy
branches.because: EC2 bills the whole instance regardless of packing, so density is the whole comparison; Fargate supports none of those four capabilities at any price

branches.if: You need Kubernetes portability, CRDs, operators or a multi-tenant platform
branches.then: EKS, with the cluster upgrade policy explicitly set to STANDARD
branches.because: EKS costs about $0.10 per cluster-hour before a pod runs and 6x that on extended support; the STANDARD upgrade policy makes AWS upgrade the cluster and removes the extended-support charge entirely

branches.if: The requirement is a container-to-URL managed service and someone suggests AWS App Runner
branches.then: Use ECS with Fargate instead
branches.because: App Runner is closed to new customers, so a new build on it has no onboarding path and a forced migration later

branches.if: Several instances or tasks must read and write the same POSIX filesystem at once
branches.then: EFS with Elastic throughput (NFS), FSx for Windows for SMB, or FSx for Lustre for HPC
branches.because: EBS is single-writer block storage; EFS is the shared POSIX option and with Elastic throughput and General Purpose mode reaches roughly 250 microsecond read latency for hot data

branches.if: One writer needs a block device
branches.then: EBS gp3 - and migrate any remaining gp2 with a live Elastic Volumes modification
branches.because: gp3 is about 20% cheaper per GiB with a flat 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s baseline at any size and no burst credits; small gp2 volumes collapse to 3 IOPS per GiB when credits exhaust

branches.if: Single-volume demand exceeds 80,000 IOPS or 2,000 MiB/s, or you need Multi-Attach or 99.999% durability
branches.then: io2 Block Express on a supported Nitro instance - but first check whether RAID-0 across several gp3 volumes is cheaper
branches.because: The gp3 ceiling is per volume, so the real fork is single-volume IOPS, and io2 provisioned IOPS are billed on top of storage

branches.if: The access pattern is object storage, append-only or write-once-read-many, and the object lifetime and access frequency are unknown
branches.then: S3 Intelligent-Tiering, plus lifecycle rules for AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload, noncurrent version expiration and expired delete markers
branches.because: Intelligent-Tiering has no minimum duration and no retrieval fee, and charges no monitoring fee for objects under 128 KB; an expiration rule alone does not reduce cost on a versioned bucket

branches.if: The object lifetime is known to be short, or the average object is under 128 KB
branches.then: Keep it in S3 Standard - do NOT transition it
branches.because: Standard-IA and One Zone-IA bill a 30-day minimum and Glacier classes 90 or 180 days, and Standard-IA, One Zone-IA and Glacier Instant Retrieval bill a 128 KB minimum per object, so an early or small transition increases cost

branches.if: The data is an archive on a recovery path with an RTO in hours
branches.then: Glacier Instant Retrieval or Glacier Flexible Retrieval, not Deep Archive
branches.because: Deep Archive Standard restore takes up to 12 hours and Bulk up to 48, with no Expedited option at all, and bulk restores are additionally capped at roughly 1,000 requests per second and 1-2 PB per day per account

branches.if: The data is derived and cheaply reproducible
branches.then: One Zone-IA or S3 Express One Zone, or instance store for scratch and spill
branches.because: Both store data in a single Availability Zone and are not resilient to losing it, and instance-store data is destroyed on stop, hibernate, terminate or host failure

branches.if: The application needs in-place partial writes or POSIX rename
branches.then: Not S3 - use EBS, EFS or FSx
branches.because: S3 has no rename, only copy-then-delete, and every small write becomes a full object rewrite; conditional writes give coordination but not POSIX semantics

decisionTrees.question: Which data store fits this workload?

branches.if: Access patterns cannot be fully enumerated, or the workload needs ad-hoc queries, joins or aggregations on non-key attributes
branches.then: A relational engine - Aurora PostgreSQL or MySQL, or RDS for engines Aurora does not support
branches.because: DynamoDB is modelled around the queries, so a new pattern needs a new index or a backfill, and the failure mode is a Scan that works in staging and burns capacity in production

branches.if: Every access is a known key-based lookup and scale or latency demands are extreme
branches.then: DynamoDB, with the partition key designed against the 3,000 RCU and 1,000 WCU per-partition-key ceiling and warm throughput configured before a known launch spike
branches.because: A single partition key value cannot span partitions, so it throttles regardless of table capacity, and on-demand scales only to double the previous observed peak

branches.if: The relational dataset will exceed 128 TiB
branches.then: Shard, archive to S3, or use Aurora Limitless - decide the shard key early
branches.because: The Aurora cluster volume has a hard 128 TiB maximum and splitting a large relational database under production load is a multi-quarter project

branches.if: The bottleneck is read throughput and the application tolerates lag
branches.then: Read replicas - Aurora Replicas if the engine allows, because they read the same cluster volume
branches.because: RDS replicas replay the write stream and can lag unboundedly under write pressure; Aurora Replicas add read capacity without write amplification. Read-after-write must still go to the writer

branches.if: The bottleneck is writes, storage IOPS or lock contention
branches.then: Scale up, offload writes to a queue, or shard - replicas will not help
branches.because: Replication is asynchronous and adding replicas adds work on RDS rather than removing it

branches.if: The requirement is availability rather than read scaling
branches.then: Multi-AZ - a Multi-AZ DB cluster or Aurora if the RTO is under a minute
branches.because: A Multi-AZ DB instance failover is documented as typical, not bounded; Multi-AZ DB clusters target about 35 seconds and Aurora typically under 30

branches.if: The workload is compute that scales far beyond the database's max_connections, such as Lambda
branches.then: RDS Proxy, or Aurora Serverless v2 or the RDS Data API for genuinely spiky work
branches.because: max_connections scales with instance memory while Lambda concurrency defaults to 1,000 per Region, and the proxy also holds connections across a failover

branches.if: The dominant query is graph traversal, columnar analytics, time series, or sub-millisecond key lookup
branches.then: Neptune; S3 with Athena or Iceberg first and Redshift when sustained query volume justifies it; Timestream for InfluxDB or Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus or TimescaleDB; ElastiCache for cache and MemoryDB when the data must survive
branches.because: Each has a data-layout requirement a row store cannot meet, and Timestream for LiveAnalytics is closed to new customers so it cannot be recommended

branches.if: Queries over open-ended document structure are genuinely needed
branches.then: DocumentDB (including Serverless) or Aurora PostgreSQL with JSONB
branches.because: Aggregation pipelines and multi-field secondary indexes over nested documents are what distinguishes a document engine from a key-value store

decisionTrees.question: How should this change reach production?

branches.if: The change touches shared persistent state - a column dropped, renamed, narrowed or made NOT NULL
branches.then: Stop. Split it into expand, migrate-and-verify, and contract releases first; no traffic-shifting strategy is sufficient without that
branches.because: Old and new code run simultaneously against one database during any rolling or blue/green deploy, so a destructive migration makes rollback impossible exactly when you need it

branches.if: The change is irreversible - data overwritten in place, a side effect already emitted, a key destroyed
branches.then: Require a tested roll-forward path, a pre-change backup with a proven restore, and a named approver; do not list rollback as the mitigation
branches.because: Rollback restores code, not consequences

branches.if: The change is schema-compatible and the bake window will contain enough events to detect the target regression rate
branches.then: Canary, with bake_time at least twice the alarm detection time
branches.because: CodeDeploy canary configurations promote on a timer, not on evidence, so a 5-minute bake against a 15-minute alarm can never fail

branches.if: Traffic is low or bursty so a small slice carries no statistical signal
branches.then: Linear, or blue/green with a full synthetic test before cutover
branches.because: The condition is required sample size at your chosen power, not a fixed requests-per-second threshold

branches.if: Duplicate capacity is affordable and instant rollback is required
branches.then: Blue/green - natively under the ECS deployment controller with lifecycle hooks, or via CodeDeploy
branches.because: Blue/green buys instant rollback at roughly 2x capacity plus a session and connection-draining problem

branches.if: The ECS service sits behind a Network Load Balancer
branches.then: Only CodeDeployDefault.ECSAllAtOnce is available through CodeDeploy - compensate with pre-deploy synthetic tests and the ECS deployment circuit breaker
branches.because: AWS documents that with an NLB, CodeDeploy for ECS supports no canary or linear configuration

branches.if: Any strategy is chosen
branches.then: Pin the image by @sha256 digest, verify the digest on ALL N targets before declaring success, and enable the ECS deployment circuit breaker with rollback
branches.because: A partial deploy produces an N-1-new-plus-1-old state nobody tested - the Knight Capital shape - and a mutable tag means the artifact tested and the artifact running can differ

decisionTrees.question: Does this workload need a second AWS Region?

branches.if: The threat model does not include regional failure and the RTO is 24 hours or more with an RPO in hours
branches.then: Single Region, multi-AZ, with Backup and Restore to a separate ACCOUNT and a proven, timed restore
branches.because: Multi-Region roughly doubles steady-state cost, dominated by inter-Region transfer and global-database replication, and a same-account backup dies with a compromised account

branches.if: Regional failure IS in the threat model and the RTO is tens of minutes with an RPO in minutes
branches.then: Pilot Light: data replicated continuously, core infrastructure pre-created but switched off, and the recovery path DEPLOYED from IaC into the DR Region recently
branches.because: Multi-AZ alone never satisfies a regional-failure RTO, and a template never deployed in the DR Region fails on Region-unavailable services, AZ names and AMI IDs

branches.if: The RTO is minutes with an RPO in seconds
branches.then: Warm Standby: a scaled-down always-on copy, with DR-Region quotas sized for projected failover peak and capacity reservations or an instance-type mix
branches.because: Warm standby relies on scaling to reach full capacity, which is a control-plane dependency during exactly the event it exists for - so pre-provision enough to carry initial traffic

branches.if: The RPO is near zero and the RTO is near real time
branches.then: Multi-Site active/active - and declare exactly one write strategy (write-global, write-local or write-partitioned) AND a conflict-detection mechanism before writing any code
branches.because: DynamoDB global tables reconcile with last-writer-wins and silently discard the loser, which is data loss when the field is a balance rather than a profile attribute

branches.if: You believe you are already multi-Region
branches.then: Enumerate every single-Region component on the critical path - identity and SSO, CI/CD, IaC state, KMS keys, secrets, container registry, observability, and the Route 53 zone you would have to change - and fix or accept each in writing
branches.because: Effective availability is that of the shared component; the Dec 2021 and Oct 2025 events hit companies whose pipeline or identity lived in us-east-1

branches.if: The failover plan requires changing IAM, Organizations, CloudFront, a Route 53 public zone or an ACM certificate for CloudFront
branches.then: Pre-create and pre-stage those resources; use ARC routing controls, pre-created Route 53 failover records with health checks, and regional STS endpoints
branches.because: Those control planes are changed only through the us-east-1 endpoint, while ARC routing controls and health-check failover are data-plane and designed to work during a us-east-1 control-plane event

branches.if: A regulator mandates multi-Region regardless of the RTO arithmetic
branches.then: Build it, and still measure the RTO by running a full evacuation exercise end to end, including failback
branches.because: A plan's status is the date of its last full test, not of its last document review - untested evacuations fail on quotas, single-Region KMS keys, uncopied images and missing secrets
